items.title: Introduction
items.text: TSE Analytics is a desktop application for analysing the data that TSE PhenoMaster, IntelliCage and IntelliMaze systems record. It imports the exports of those systems, keeps every dataset of a study together in one workspace, and offers a toolbox of plots and statistical analyses whose results go into reports you can share.

items.title: What you can do
items.text:
• Manage several datasets at once. Import one export after another, merge trials into one dataset, and save the whole workspace to come back to it later.
  • Get the metadata for free. Animals, their properties, the recorded variables with units and the sample interval are extracted from the export during import.
  • Shape the data before analysing it. Resample, trim the time range, exclude time spans or animals, define factors that group animals (by hand, by an animal property, by time of day, by elapsed time or by interval), detect outliers, and derive new datatables without touching the original.
  • Analyse with a large toolbox. Line and facet plots, histograms, distributions and normality tests, correlation and regression, the ANOVA family and linear mixed models, correlation matrices, PCA, t-SNE, MDS and UMAP, chronobiology (actograms, periodograms), time-series decomposition and autocorrelation, and IntelliCage-specific analyses. Every tool runs in the background and can be cancelled.
  • Look at the raw recordings. Dedicated viewers for PhenoMaster DrinkFeed, Calo, ActiMot and Group Housing data.
  • Write reports. A rich-text editor per report; every analysis, the data table and the fast line plot add their result to a report with one click. Reports export to HTML and print to PDF.
  • Automate with pipelines and ask an AI assistant about the open workspace (both optional features, see Pipelines and AI assistance).

Everything runs on your computer. Nothing leaves it unless you enable the TSE Assistant with a cloud model or connect an assistant through the MCP server — what such an assistant reads goes to its provider.

items.title: Supported data sources
items.text: Source What TSE Analytics reads PhenoMaster The .tse export of the PhenoMaster software, with its DrinkFeed, Calo (indirect calorimetry), ActiMot (activity) and Group Housing tables. IntelliCage The IntelliCage export (.zip): visits and nosepokes, with transition, place-preference and learning-curve analyses. IntelliMaze The IntelliMaze export (.zip): animal gates, consumption scales, running wheels, operant devices and the IntelliCage module, with a merged CSV export.

items.title: How this manual is organised
items.text:
• Installation and Get started take you from the installer to the first analysis: the main window, the menus, workspaces, importing and exporting data.
  • Workspace tree, Dataset details and Data table explain how the data is organised and prepared.
  • Toolbox documents every analysis tool, Extension viewers the PhenoMaster viewers, and IntelliCage and IntelliMaze the two other systems.
  • Reports, Pipelines, AI assistance and Settings cover the rest; the Reference lists the predefined variables, the log and the keyboard shortcuts.

Note

The manual describes the desktop application. Its pages open from Help ▸ Documentation inside the app (the copy that ships with the app, or online — see Settings).

items.title: Installation
items.text: TSE Analytics is installed from a file that TSE Systems provides: an installer on Windows, an AppImage on Linux. If you do not have it, contact TSE Service.

items.title: System requirements
items.text:
• Operating system: Windows 10 or 11 (64-bit), or a 64-bit Linux desktop distribution with glibc 2.34 or newer (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12, Fedora 36, RHEL 9 or newer).
  • Processor: four cores or more; a high clock speed helps, because most analyses run on one core.
  • Memory: 16 GB or more. Some analyses, ActiMot in particular, need more for long recordings.
  • Display: 1920 × 1080 or larger.
  • Storage: an SSD, with about 1 GB for the application and 10 GB or more free for data and workspaces.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
1. Double-click tse-analytics-setup-<version>.exe.
  2. Choose the installation folder or keep the default, TSE Systems\TSE Analytics <version> in your user profile's Programs folder. The application installs for the current user only and needs no administrator rights.
  3. Finish the wizard. It creates a Start menu entry under TSE Systems and a desktop shortcut, both named TSE Analytics version.

Every version installs next to the others, in its own folder with its own shortcuts, so you can keep several versions and return to an earlier one. Only one runs at a time: starting another version while one is open brings the open one to the front.

The installer also registers the .workspace file type, so a double-click on a workspace file opens it in TSE Analytics, and adds an Open with entry for .duckdb workspaces. Both open the version you installed last.

To update, install the new version and remove the old one when you no longer need it. To remove a version, use Settings ▸ Apps (or Programs and Features) and uninstall its entry, TSE Analytics version. Removing any version also removes the .workspace and .duckdb file types; run the installer of the version you keep again to restore them.

items.title: Linux
items.text:
1. Make the file executable and start it:

    chmod +x tse-analytics-<version>-x86_64.AppImage
./tse-analytics-<version>-x86_64.AppImage

  2. There is nothing else to install; the AppImage carries everything. If your system has no FUSE, start it with the option --appimage-extract-and-run.

The AppImage registers the .workspace file type for its session, so tse-analytics study.workspace and a double-click in the file manager open the file. To update, replace the file; to remove the application, delete it.

items.title: First start
items.text:
The window first shows Starting the analysis engine… while the analysis server starts on your computer. The first start after an installation can take up to a minute; later starts are faster. The main window then appears with an empty workspace — continue with Get started.

If the engine fails to start, the window says so and offers Restart, Open log folder and Quit. The log folder holds the application log, which TSE Service may ask for; see Log and troubleshooting.

Tip

Save your workspaces before uninstalling or replacing the application. Workspace files are ordinary files in the folders you chose; the application never deletes them.

items.title: Settings
items.text: File ▸ Settings… opens the settings of the application. They are stored on the computer that runs TSE Analytics, not in a workspace, and apply to every workspace you open there. Change what you need and click Save; a value that is out of range is marked and the dialog jumps to it.

items.title: General
items.text:
• Help mode — where Help ▸ Documentation goes: Use offline help, the default, opens the copy that ships with the application (the same version as the application, no internet needed), Use online help the manual on the web.
  • Plots — DPI, Width (in) and Height (in): the resolution and size of the figures the analysis tools draw when they are added to a report or exported. On screen a figure fills its panel.
  • Enable internal features — turns on features still in development: the Pipelines and TSE Assistant menus, the import of CSV files and of extension data from CSV. Off by default.

items.title: TSE Assistant
items.text:
Shown when internal features are enabled. See AI assistance.

  • Anthropic API key — the key the assistant uses for the Claude models. It is stored on this computer; Remove key forgets it. A key set in the environment variable ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is used when none is stored here.
  • Default model — the model a new conversation starts with: a Claude model, or a model of a local LM Studio server.
  • LM Studio host — the address of that server.
  • Let the TSE Assistant search the web and read web pages — on by default: a Claude model may search the web and read the pages you name, for example a paper whose methods you ask it to apply. The searches and the pages it reads go through Anthropic's servers and become part of the conversation; web searches cost $10 per 1,000 plus the tokens they add. Turn it off to keep the assistant off the web. LM Studio models never search the web.

items.title: AI permissions
items.text:
These apply to the TSE Assistant and to every assistant connected through the MCP server, whether or not the server is running. See AI permissions and the Python sandbox.

  • Allow AI assistants to change the workspace — on by default: assistants may also import data, open and save workspaces, edit factors and outliers, and create datatables and pipelines. Destructive steps still ask you first. Off, assistants only read and analyse.
  • Run Python code — Off, Ask before each run (you read the code before it runs) or Run without asking, the default. The code runs in a separate, guarded Python process with the open datatables.
  • Time limit per run (s) and Memory limit per Python session (MB) — how long one run may take and how much memory a Python session may use; shown while Run Python code is not Off.

items.title: MCP server
items.text:
• Let external AI assistants (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, …) use this app — starts a server other assistants connect to. Once it is on and saved, the section shows the endpoint, the token and ready-to-copy configuration for the common clients. See MCP server.

Note

The defaults of the CSV import (delimiter, decimal separator, date format) are not set here: tick Remember as default in the import dialog itself.

items.title: AI assistance
items.text:
TSE Analytics can put an AI assistant to work on the open workspace in two ways: the built-in TSE Assistant, a chat panel inside the application, and the MCP server, through which an assistant you already use — Claude Code, Claude Desktop or another MCP client — connects to the application. Both see the same tools: they read the datasets, run the analyses of the toolbox and save results into reports, and — unless you turn it off — change the workspace and run their own Python code.

Note

The TSE Assistant is an internal feature (Settings ▸ General ▸ Enable internal features). Everything an assistant reads leaves your computer through that assistant's provider — with the TSE Assistant, through the model you choose; with the MCP server, through the connected client. With web access on, the TSE Assistant's search queries go to the search provider as well.

items.title: The TSE Assistant
items.text:
Assistant ▸ Open TSE Assistant opens the chat panel. Ask about the open workspace in plain language — Compare the drinking of the treatment groups — and the assistant looks at the datasets, runs the analysis tools, and answers with its figures and tables in the chat, each tool call shown as a card you can expand.

  • Model — a Claude model (with your Anthropic API key from Settings) or a model served by a local LM Studio.
  • Clear starts a new conversation; Add Report saves the conversation as a report of a dataset; Save as Pipeline asks the assistant to save a pipeline that reproduces the results of the conversation, so you can run them again later (Pipelines).
  • Python session — when running code is allowed, the assistant writes and runs Python on the open datatables in a separate Python session whose variables persist from run to run; Restart ends it. Its figures draw the animals and the factor levels in their colours from the Factors tab.
  • Web access — with Let the TSE Assistant search the web and read web pages on in Settings (the default), a Claude model can read the pages you link and search the web: paste the address of a paper and ask the assistant to apply its methods. Each search or page it reads appears as a card with the pages it found; the parts of an answer that rest on a search end with numbered links to their sources. Some sites refuse automated access (ResearchGate, for instance); the assistant then looks for an open-access copy, such as the article on PubMed Central, and says which one it read.
  • Enter sends, Shift+Enter starts a new line; Stop interrupts an answer.

items.title: What an assistant may do
items.text: AI permissions and the Python sandbox explains the two switches that decide what assistants may change and whether they may run code, and the approval dialog that asks you before a destructive step.

items.title: Assistants outside the application
items.text: MCP server explains how to connect Claude Code, Claude Desktop or another client.

items.title: MCP server
items.text: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is how AI assistants such as Claude Code and Claude Desktop connect to applications. With the MCP server on, an assistant you already use can inspect the open workspace, run the analysis tools, save reports, and — with the permissions you grant — prepare the workspace and run code, exactly like the TSE Assistant.

items.title: Turning it on
items.text:
Settings ▸ MCP server ▸ Let external AI assistants use this app, then Save. The section then shows what a client needs:

  • Endpoint — the local address of the server, with a copy button.
  • Token — the key a client presents; shown masked, with Copy and Regenerate…. Regenerating cuts off every client configured with the old token.
  • Connect a client — the configuration to paste, ready for Claude Code (an HTTP connection, or the application's own launcher for clients that start their servers), Claude Desktop (its configuration file, with the path for your operating system) and Other clients.

The server listens on your computer only. Its token opens nothing but the MCP endpoint, and the launch token of the window is never shared.

items.title: What the assistant sees
items.text: The same tools as the TSE Assistant: the workspace tree, the metadata and data of every datatable, the catalogue of analysis tools with their settings, the reports. Results come back as text and images; large tables are summarised. What the assistant may change is set in AI permissions, and the approval dialog appears in the application window while the assistant waits.

items.title: Building pipelines
items.text:
With internal features on and Allow AI assistants to change the workspace allowed, an assistant can build pipelines as well as run them:

  • list_pipeline_nodes — the nodes a pipeline is built from, and the settings of the ones it needs.
  • get_pipeline — a saved pipeline in full, in the form save_pipeline takes back.
  • save_pipeline — creates a pipeline, or replaces one. It checks the whole graph first — the node types, the connections, every setting against the data that reaches its node — and lists every problem at once, so nothing half-built is saved. Replacing an existing pipeline asks you; if it is open in the editor, its unsaved changes are replaced when you agree.
  • run_pipeline — runs it and reports every node, with the statistics the analyses publish.
  • set_animal_properties — stores per-animal values such as lean and fat mass from a body-composition scan, or a genotype, as animal properties; a pipeline turns them into covariates.

Ask, for example: Implement the workflow described in https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236072062 in a new pipeline. Claude Code and Claude Desktop read the article themselves; ResearchGate refuses automated access, so they fall back on the open-access copy on PubMed Central. The assistant maps the method's steps to nodes, asks you what the paper leaves open — the variable, the covariate, the grouping factor — saves the pipeline with the steps in the node captions and the paper in its description, and runs it. Example: the 39 steps shows the result.

The server also offers these steps as the prompt pipeline_from_method; Claude Code lists it as the command /mcp__tse-analytics__pipeline_from_method. The TSE Assistant has the same tools, and with web access on it reads the paper too (see AI assistance).

items.title: AI permissions and the Python sandbox
items.text: Settings ▸ AI permissions decides what every assistant — the TSE Assistant and the clients of the MCP server — may do beyond reading and analysing.
path: AI permissions and the Python sandbox

items.title: Reading and analysing
items.text: Without any permission an assistant can list the datasets, read metadata and data, run every analysis tool and save results into reports. It cannot change the data.
path: AI permissions and the Python sandbox

items.title: Changing the workspace
items.text:
Allow AI assistants to change the workspace, on by default, lets an assistant import data, open and save workspaces, edit factors, animal properties and outlier settings, and create datatables and pipelines — the steps a colleague would take to prepare an analysis. Steps that destroy something (deleting a datatable or a factor, overwriting a file, replacing a pipeline) still ask you first:

The dialog names the assistant and the step; Deny or the step's own button decide, and no answer within the countdown counts as a denial. The window flashes and the title says (Confirm) while a request waits.
path: AI permissions and the Python sandbox

items.title: Running Python code
items.text:
Run Python code lets an assistant write and run its own Python on the open datatables, for a plot or a calculation the toolbox does not offer:

  • Off — assistants cannot run code.
  • Ask before each run — the code is shown in an approval dialog; you read it before it runs.
  • Run without asking — the default.

The code runs in a separate, guarded Python process — the sandbox — with a timeout and a memory limit you set. The process cannot write into the workspace except through the same tools the assistant has anyway. The guard is a safeguard against mistakes, not a security boundary: allow code only from assistants you trust, or choose Ask before each run to read it first.

The setting also governs the Python nodes of pipelines — the code an assistant keeps when it saves a conversation as a pipeline:

  • Off — Python nodes fail with a message, and an assistant cannot save a pipeline with Python nodes.
  • Ask before each run — when an assistant runs such a pipeline, the approval dialog shows the code of every Python node first.
  • Run without asking — the code runs.

A run you start in the pipeline editor never asks: you start it yourself, and the code is in the node's properties.

items.title: Data table
items.text: Double-click a datatable in the tree (or choose Toolbox ▸ Data ▸ Table) to open it as a panel: the rows on the left, the Variables pane on the right.

items.title: Columns
items.text:
• DateTime — the time stamp of the row; Timedelta — the time since the start of the recording.
  • Box and Animal — where and from whom the row was recorded (an IntelliCage or IntelliMaze table has its own identifying columns).
  • One column per factor with the level the row falls into — Total, LightCycle, the dataset's own factors, Trial for a merged dataset.
  • One column per variable that is ticked in the Variables pane, with the unit in the pane. <NA> marks a missing value.

Drag the right border of a header to change a column's width; double-click it to fit the column to its content. A table opens with its columns fitted to the first rows, and the widths you change are remembered for that datatable.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
• Export — the table as CSV or Excel; see Exporting data.
  • Filter — a pandas query such as Weight > 25, Box == 1 or Drink > 0 and LightCycle == "Dark"; press Enter to apply it. The count on the right shows how many rows match and how many the table holds; the table shows a window of them and loads more as you scroll.
  • Delete values — sets the selected cells to missing. Click a cell to select it, Shift-click another to select the block between them, Ctrl-click (Cmd on macOS) to add or remove cells, or drag across cells; the arrow keys move the selection, Shift with an arrow extends it, and Esc clears it. The change is part of the workspace once you save it.
  • Fit columns — fits every column to the rows loaded so far.
  • Table Info and Descriptive Statistics — see Descriptive statistics.

Click a column header to sort by it, and again to reverse the order.

Note

The filter, the sort order and the ticked variables change what you see and what Export writes. The analyses do not use them: a tool reads the whole datatable with the variables you choose in its settings.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Variables — units, aggregation, and which variables the table shows
  • Outliers — highlighting or removing outliers
  • Adding a variable

items.title: Adding a variable
items.text:
The + button of the Variables pane adds a variable to the datatable, computed from what is already there. The new variable behaves like any other: it shows in the table, has an aggregation, and every analysis can use it.

  • Name, Unit, Description — how the variable appears.
  • Aggregation — how it is combined when rows are aggregated (see Variables).
  • Origin — where the values come from:
    • Animal property — every row gets the value of the chosen property of its animal, for example the weight, so it can serve as a covariate in an ANCOVA.
    • Cumulative variable — the running total of a variable per animal.
    • Differential variable — the difference between consecutive rows of a variable per animal, turning a running total back into per-interval amounts.
    • Expression — a formula over the variables of the row, such as Feed / Drink or Weight * 2.

Click Add. The variable is stored in the datatable and saved with the workspace.

items.title: Descriptive statistics and table info
items.text: Two buttons in the data table's toolbar describe the datatable without running an analysis.

items.title: Descriptive Statistics
items.text: For every variable shown in the table: the number of values (count), the mean and standard deviation, the minimum, the quartiles (25%, 50% — the median — and 75%) and the maximum, computed over the whole datatable with the dataset's outlier settings applied. Add Report puts the table into a report of the dataset (see Reports).

items.title: Table Info
items.text: The technical summary of the datatable: the number of rows, and for every column the number of non-missing values and the data type. A column with fewer non-missing values than rows has gaps — in a PhenoMaster table the calorimetry variables, which are only measured while the box is sampled.

items.title: Outliers
items.text: Outlier detection marks or removes values that fall far outside the rest of a variable's distribution — a measurement error, a sensor glitch, a cage that was opened. It is set per datatable in the Outliers popover of the Variables pane, and applies to the variables ticked in the pane's Outliers column.

items.title: Mode
items.text:
• Outliers detection off — nothing is marked (the default).
  • Highlight outliers — the table marks the outlying cells; the values stay and the analyses use them.
  • Remove outliers — the outlying cells are treated as missing in the table and in every analysis of the datatable. The other values of the same row are kept.

items.title: Detection type
items.text:
• Interquartile Range (IQR) — the classic rule: with the quartiles Q1 and Q3 of the variable and the multiplier k (1.5 by default), a value is an outlier when it lies below Q1 − k × IQR or above Q3 + k × IQR. A smaller multiplier marks more values.
  • Z-Score — a value is an outlier when it lies more than three standard deviations from the mean of the variable.
  • Thresholds — fixed bounds: tick Min threshold and Max threshold and enter the values a valid measurement must stay within.

items.title: Freezing
items.text:
Freeze outliers removal applies the current removal to the datatable for good: the removed values become missing values in the data, and the detection can be switched off again without bringing them back.

Warning

Freezing cannot be undone. Clone the datatable first if you may need the original values.

items.title: See also
items.text: • Variables — the Outliers column that chooses the variables

items.title: Variables
items.text:
The pane on the right of a data table lists its variables. It decides which columns the table shows, how each variable is aggregated, and which variables the outlier detection looks at.

  • Show — tick the variables the table displays and exports. The choice is remembered per datatable.
  • Name and Unit — from the export; PhenoMaster variables come with their unit and description (see Predefined variables in the Reference).
  • Aggregation — how the variable is combined when rows are aggregated: when a datatable is resampled, and when an analysis groups rows by a factor. mean, median, sum, min or max. PhenoMaster variables get a sensible default — mean for a rate or a concentration (VO2, RER, Temp), sum for an amount per bin (Drink, Feed, DistD), max for a running total (DistK). Change it when your question needs another summary.
  • Outliers — tick the variables the outlier detection applies to.

Click a column header to sort the list by it, and again to reverse the order. Drag the right border of a header to change a column's width, or double-click it to fit the column to its content; the widths are remembered for that datatable.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
• Outliers opens the outlier settings.
  • Reset restores the default aggregation and outlier flags of a PhenoMaster table.
  • The select-all and deselect-all icons tick every variable or none. With none ticked, the table and the export keep only the Animal, DateTime and factor columns; tick the few variables you want from there.
  • The fit icon fits every column to its content.
  • + adds a variable computed from the data; see Adding a variable.
  • The trash icon deletes the selected variables from the datatable.

Tip

A cumulative variable such as DistK reports, with max, the total reached by the end of each interval. For the activity within each interval use its differential twin (DistD with sum), or add one with Add Variable ▸ Differential variable.

items.title: Dataset details
items.text:
Below the workspace tree, three tabs describe the dataset that is selected in the tree: Info (its metadata), Animals (its animals and their properties) and Factors (how the animals and the time are grouped). Every datatable, analysis and viewer of the dataset uses these.

  • Info — the metadata the export carries.
  • Animals — the animals, their properties, and how to edit them.
  • Factors — factors and levels, the built-in factors, and the Factors dialog.
  • Time grouping — how the time axis is grouped: light and dark cycles, phases, intervals, trials.

items.title: Animals
items.text: The Animals tab lists every animal of the selected dataset with its properties — for a PhenoMaster export the box, the weight and the text fields entered in PhenoMaster; for IntelliCage and IntelliMaze exports what their metadata holds.

items.title: Editing
items.text:
• Double-click a cell to edit it: the animal's id in the Animal column, or a property. A value that reads as a number is stored as a number. A renamed animal keeps its colour and its place in the lists, and its factors follow the new id.
  • Add property adds a column with a name you choose; fill it in cell by cell.
  • Delete property removes the selected column. A property a factor is built on cannot go without a warning — the factor would lose its levels.

items.title: Sorting and columns
items.text:
• Click a column header to sort by it, again to reverse the order, and a third time for the original order. The tab opens sorted by the animal id.
  • Drag the right border of a header to change a column's width; double-click it to fit the column to its content, or Fit columns in the toolbar to fit every column. The tab opens with its columns fitted, and the widths you change are remembered for that dataset.

Properties are the base of Animal property factors: a property such as Sex, Genotype or Treatment turns into a factor with one level per distinct value in the Factors dialog. Change a value and the factors made from the property follow: their levels are rebuilt, and each level keeps its colour.

Numeric properties — the body mass, lean and fat mass from a body-composition scan — become covariates of an ANCOVA through Add Variable or a pipeline's Add Variable node.

items.title: Properties set by an AI assistant
items.text: An assistant allowed to change the workspace can fill in properties for many animals at once with set_animal_properties — lean and fat mass you paste into the conversation, say, or a genotype read from a text field. A property new to the dataset reaches every animal, empty where no value was given; the assistant reports the previous values, so a change can be undone. See MCP server.

items.title: Excluding animals
items.text: The Animals tab does not filter the data: every analysis sees all animals of the dataset. To leave animals out, either exclude them from the dataset for good (Edit Dataset) or derive a datatable without them (Edit Datatable). Plots offer an animal filter of their own where it makes sense (the fast line plot, for example).

items.title: Factors
items.text:
A factor groups the rows of a dataset into levels: the animals by genotype or treatment, the time by light and dark cycle, by phase or by interval, the trials of a merged dataset. Every analysis lets you group by a factor, and the ANOVA family and the mixed models take factors as their independent variables.

The Factors tab lists the factors of the selected dataset with their role, and each level with its colour and the number of animals in it.

items.title: Built-in factors
items.text:
Every dataset has three factors you cannot delete:

  • Animal — one level per animal; grouping by it shows the animals separately. Its levels hold the animals' colours: every plot of an animal draws it in its colour, whatever the plot is grouped by, and so do the figures of the TSE Assistant. Its levels follow the animals — renaming or excluding an animal changes them — so the Factors dialog lets you change only their colours.
  • Total — a single level, All animals; grouping by it pools everything.
  • LightCycle — Light and Dark, from the time of day. Its light and dark cycle start times are set in the Factors dialog (see Time grouping).

Animal and Total only group: the plots offer them under Group by, but the analyses that compare the levels of a factor — the ANOVAs, ANCOVA, the Linear Mixed Model and the non-parametric tests — do not offer them as their Factor. Each level of Animal is a single animal and Total has one level, so there is nothing to compare: add a factor of your own, such as the genotype or the treatment group.

A merged dataset also gets Trial (see Merging datasets).

items.title: Roles
items.text: A factor is between-subject when each animal belongs to one level for the whole recording (genotype, treatment group), and within-subject when the same animal passes through several levels over time (light and dark, the phases of a protocol, the trials). The repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVAs need this distinction.

items.title: The Factors dialog
items.text:
Edit Factors opens the dialog: the factors on the left, the levels of the selected factor in the middle, its configuration on the right. Click OK to apply every change at once.

Adding a factor. Type a name, choose the Kind, click Add:

Kind Levels come from Configuration Animal-based your choice Add levels, then tick the animals of each level. An animal belongs to one level at most. Animal property a property of the animals (Text1, Sex, a property you added) Choose the property and click Extract levels: one level per distinct value, with its animals. Time phases phases of the recording Rows of phase name and start (hours after the recording start); Add phase / delete. Time interval equal intervals The Interval (hours); levels Hour 0, Hour 1, … are generated for the dataset's time range. Column the values of a column of the data Choose the column.

Rename and Delete act on the selected factor; the built-in ones are protected. Role sets between- or within-subject.

Levels. Add level and Delete level for animal-based factors; click a level's colour swatch to change the colour every plot uses for it. The count in brackets is the number of animals in the level.

items.title: Colours
items.text:
Each level has a colour, and every plot draws the level in it: the toolbox plots, the viewers' plots, the fast line plot and the TSE Assistant's figures. Change a colour with the swatch next to a level in the Factors tab, or in the dialog: the open plots redraw at once, and the next analysis, pipeline run or assistant figure uses the new colour. A report keeps the colours it was made with. A new factor gives its levels the chart colours — eight vivid colours — and a factor with more than eight levels the animals' long list, so no two levels share a colour.

Note

Give every factor at least two levels with animals in them; an analysis that groups by a factor with one level has nothing to compare.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Time grouping — the factors that group the time axis, and the light cycle settings
  • Animals — the properties the Animal property kind reads

items.title: Info
items.text:
The Info tab shows the metadata of the selected dataset as a tree you can fold and unfold.

For a PhenoMaster export it holds what the PhenoMaster software wrote: the experiment (software version, the experiment number and file, its start and end, the user and the free-text fields, the recording interval and the runtime), the animals with their properties, and the variables of the tables. IntelliCage and IntelliMaze exports show what their formats provide.

The Info tab is read-only. Animals and their properties are edited in the Animals tab; the name and the time range of the dataset in the Edit Dataset dialog.

items.title: Time grouping
items.text: Recordings run for days at a fine interval. Three things shape the time axis before an analysis sees it: the sample interval of the datatable, the factors that group the time, and the aggregation of each variable.

items.title: Sample interval: resampling
items.text: A datatable keeps the interval it was recorded at (one minute, for example). To analyse it per hour or per day, derive a resampled datatable (Deriving a datatable) or resample the whole dataset (Editing a dataset). Each variable is aggregated into the new interval with its own aggregation — mean for a rate such as VO2, sum for an amount such as Drink, max for a running total such as DistK (see Variables).

items.title: Grouping the time with factors
items.text:
Most tools have a Group by choice: Animal, one of the factors, or Total. A factor whose levels are time spans groups the rows by when they were recorded:

  • LightCycle (built-in) — Light and Dark, from the time of day. Set Light cycle start and Dark cycle start in the Factors dialog when the facility's lighting differs from the default.
  • Time phases — phases you define by name and start time, such as baseline, fasting and refeeding.
  • Time interval — equal intervals of a chosen number of hours, numbered from the start of the recording.

These are within-subject factors: every animal passes through every level. Compare their levels with the repeated measures ANOVA or the non-parametric tests, or combine them with a between-subject factor in the mixed-design ANOVA or the Linear Mixed Model to test, for example, whether a treatment acts differently in the dark phase.

items.title: Trials
items.text: A merged dataset carries a Trial factor and column (Merging datasets). Group by it to compare the trials, or by Total to pool them.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Factors — kinds, roles and the Factors dialog
  • Data table — the columns the grouping produces

items.title: Extension viewers
items.text:
A PhenoMaster export can carry more than the Main table: the raw recordings of the DrinkFeed, Calo, ActiMot and Group Housing extensions, imported as the tables you tick in the import dialog. They appear under Raw Data in the tree with a puzzle icon, and each opens in its own viewer — a panel with tabs for the raw data, the processed results and the plots, and a side panel with the selectors and settings.

Viewer Raw table What it does DrinkFeed drinkfeed_bin, drinkfeed_raw Turns drinking and feeding registrations into meals (episodes) or fixed intervals, with intake per diet Calo calo_bin Fits the gas exchange of each box against its reference box and predicts the calorimetry between measurements ActiMot actimot_raw Reconstructs the trajectory of an animal from the light-beam frames, with smoothing, and plots it Group Housing group_housing Cleans the TraffiCage registrations of a group-housing box and shows the activity and a heatmap per animal

Every viewer runs its calculation in the background and shows the result in its tabs; the DrinkFeed and Group Housing viewers can store their results as a datatable of the dataset (Add Datatable), where the toolbox can analyse them. The settings you apply are remembered per viewer; the selections (boxes, bins, animals) are not.

items.title: ActiMot
items.text: The ActiMot extension records the light-beam frame of a box many times per second. The ActiMot viewer turns the frames of one box into the trajectory of its animal — position, displacement, speed and acceleration — and plots it.

items.title: Side panel
items.text:
• Boxes — choose one box (its animal and factor levels are shown); the viewer works on one box at a time.
  • Settings — Savitzky–Golay smoothing of the trajectory with its Window size (odd) and Polynomial order; Reset settings restores the defaults.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
• Preprocess builds the trajectory of the chosen box with the current settings. The raw frames of a long recording are large; the processing runs in the background and can take a while.
  • Variable — what the Events Plot shows.

items.title: Tabs
items.text:
• Events — the beam events of the box as recorded.
  • Frames — the 32 × 64 beam mask of any frame with the centroid of the animal; step through the frames.
  • Events Plot — after preprocessing: the trajectory, a stream plot or a heatmap of the positions, with the plot's own options (the number of points, the bins, normalisation, a log scale).

Note

ActiMot data is large: the raw table of a four-day recording has tens of millions of rows, and preprocessing needs several gigabytes of memory. Import it only when you need it.

items.title: Calo
items.text: Indirect calorimetry measures the oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production of a box at intervals, one box after another, against a reference box. The Calo viewer fits the gas exchange of every box to a curve so that the values between the measurements can be predicted, and reports the predicted energy expenditure.

items.title: Side panel
items.text:
• Boxes — the boxes that have a reference box; tick the ones to fit.
  • Bins — the measurement bins to include.
  • Settings — the fitting parameters: the number of iterations, the prediction offset, the flow (taken from the Main table when it records one), and for O2 and CO2 the training window and the bounds of the curve parameters.

items.title: Toolbar and tabs
items.text:
• Calculate prediction for selected boxes — fits every ticked box (in parallel) and writes one result table per box with the measured and predicted O2, CO2, RER and energy expenditure (EE-p).
  • Data — the raw calorimetry bins: O2, CO2, VO2, VCO2, RER, EE and the marker per bin and offset, with the same filter, variables pane and export as any data table.
  • Plot — the chosen Variable of every box over time, each box in the colour of its animal, with the overview below.
  • Test — the test fit of one box: Calculate Test Fit fits the O2 and CO2 curves and reports how fast the box settles (T90, T95, T99), with the measured and the fitted points, so the settings can be checked before fitting everything; Export training data writes the training window as CSV.
  • RER — after Calculate prediction for selected boxes: for the chosen Box, the measured and the predicted value of the chosen Variable (RER, O2, Ref.O2, CO2, Ref.CO2, VO2, VCO2 or EE) over the bins, in two colours.

items.title: DrinkFeed
items.text: The DrinkFeed viewer turns the drinking and feeding registrations of the DrinkFeed extension into meals and intake: either episodes — bouts of drinking or feeding separated by pauses — or fixed intervals, per animal and per diet.

items.title: Side panel
items.text:
• Animals — tick the animals to analyse (Select all animals ticks every one), and choose the diet of each animal from the diets you define in the settings. Click a column header to sort the list; drag a header's right border to change a column's width.
  • Settings — the analysis mode and its parameters:
    • Sequential analysis (episodes) — registrations closer together than the pause you set form one episode; the parameters define the minimum episode and the maximum gap.
    • Fixed intervals — the intake is summed per interval of the length you set.
    • Diets — a list of diets with their caloric value, so the intake is reported in kilocalories as well as in grams and millilitres. Add diet and Delete diet edit the list.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
• Calculate runs the analysis for the ticked animals with the current settings.
  • Add Datatable stores the result — the episodes or the intervals, one row per animal and episode or interval — as a datatable of the dataset, so the toolbox can analyse it.

items.title: Tabs
items.text:
• Raw Data and Raw Data Plot — the registrations as imported, and as a plot per animal.
  • Intervals and Intervals Plots — with the fixed-interval mode: the intake per interval, as a table and as plots.
  • Events — with the sequential mode: every drinking or feeding event.
  • Episodes and Episodes Timeline — the episodes with their start, duration and amount, and a timeline per animal, each in its colour.
  • Inter-meal Intervals — the distribution of the pauses between episodes, per animal in its colour.
  • Intake — the total intake per animal and diet, in mass, volume and kilocalories.

items.title: Group Housing
items.text: In a group-housing box several animals share the cage, and the TraffiCage system registers which animal is at which device. The Group Housing viewer cleans those registrations and shows the activity and the presence of every animal.

items.title: Side panel
items.text: • Animals — tick the animals to show in the plots.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
• Table — which raw table the Raw Data tab shows.
  • Overlap time difference — registrations of the same animal closer together than this are merged, and overlapping registrations of different animals are resolved.
  • Preprocess cleans the registrations (repeated records removed, overlaps resolved) into the All, TraffiCage and DrinkFeed tables.
  • Add Datatable stores the preprocessed TraffiCage table as a datatable of the dataset.

items.title: Tabs
items.text:
• Raw Data — the registrations as imported.
  • Preprocessed Data — the cleaned tables.
  • Activity — the registrations of the ticked animals over time.
  • Heatmap — where each animal spent its time.

items.title: The main window
items.text: The main window has a fixed layout: the menu bar on top, the workspace tree and the dataset details on the left, the panels you open in the centre, an optional log pane below them, and a status bar at the bottom.

items.title: Header
items.text: The header holds the menu bar — File, View, Toolbox, Help, and Assistant and Pipeline when internal features are enabled — and, on the right, the theme toggle, which cycles between the light theme, the dark theme and the system setting. Menus and shortcuts lists every command.

items.title: Sidebar
items.text:
The sidebar shows the Datasets tree on top and three tabs below it:

  • Datasets lists every dataset of the workspace with its datatables, raw data, reports and pipelines. Select an item to work with it; double-click a datatable to open it. The toolbar above the tree imports, edits, clones, deletes and merges. See Workspace tree.
  • Info shows the metadata of the selected dataset, Animals its animals and their properties, Factors its factors and levels. See Dataset details.

View ▸ Toggle Sidebar hides and shows it; drag its right edge to resize it.

items.title: Panels
items.text:
Everything you open — a data table, a plot, an analysis, a report, a viewer, a pipeline — is a panel, and every panel is a tab in the centre. Open as many as you like, switch between them, and close a tab with its × or a middle-click. A panel remembers its settings while it is open.

The panels belong to the window: they survive a reload of the window, and a new start of the application begins with none.

items.title: Log pane
items.text: View ▸ Toggle Log shows the application log below the panels: what was imported, how long an analysis took, and every warning or error. Choose the lowest level to show, clear it, or hide it again with its ×. See Log and troubleshooting.

items.title: Status bar
items.text: From left to right: the connection to the analysis engine, the workspace file name (or Unsaved workspace) with a • when there are unsaved changes, the task that is running, and on the right the memory the engine uses and the version.

items.title: How the data is organised
items.text:
Workspace                       one file: study.workspace or study.duckdb
├── Dataset                     one import (or a merge of several)
│   ├── Main                    the datatable every analysis starts from
│   ├── derived datatables      resampled, trimmed or filtered copies you create
│   ├── Raw Data                the extension tables of the export (DrinkFeed, Calo, …)
│   ├── Reports                 your reports for this dataset
│   └── Pipelines               your pipelines for this dataset (internal feature)
└── Dataset …

A workspace holds any number of datasets. A dataset is one import: its animals, factors and variables, its Main datatable, the datatables you derive from it, the raw extension tables of the export, and its reports. Every analysis works on one datatable and sees the dataset's animals, factors and outlier settings.

items.title: Background tasks
items.text: Importing, merging, running an analysis or a pipeline and exporting take time, so they run in the background. A message in the lower right corner shows the progress and lets you cancel; the status bar names the running task. You can keep working while a task runs.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Menus and shortcuts
  • Workspaces
  • Importing data

items.title: Exporting data
items.text: Every result leaves TSE Analytics as a file: table data as CSV or Excel, analysis results as Excel or CSV, reports as HTML, pipelines as JSON. On the desktop each export opens a Save as dialog (in your Downloads folder by default) and confirms with Saved … when the file is written.

items.title: Table data
items.text: Open a datatable (double-click it in the tree, or Toolbox ▸ Data ▸ Table) and choose Export ▸ Export to CSV or Export to Excel. The file holds what the table shows: the selected variables, the rows that pass the filter, in the current sort order, with the dataset's outlier settings applied. See Data table.

items.title: Analysis results
items.text: Every analysis tool has a Results menu once it has run: Download Excel writes all result tables into one workbook, Download CSV one table, and Add as Datatable… turns a result table into a datatable of the dataset for further analysis. See Toolbox.

items.title: Reports
items.text: A report exports to a standalone HTML file (Export HTML) that opens in any browser, and prints through Print — choose Print to PDF (Windows: Microsoft Print to PDF) in the print dialog for a PDF. See Reports.

items.title: Pipelines
items.text: A pipeline exports to a JSON file (Export in the pipeline panel or the tree) that another workspace imports with Pipeline ▸ Import Pipeline…. See Pipelines.

items.title: IntelliMaze merged CSV
items.text: For an IntelliMaze dataset, File ▸ Export Merged CSV… writes the registrations of the selected extensions into one CSV file in the format other IntelliMaze tools read. See IntelliMaze.

items.title: See also
items.text: • Importing data

items.title: Importing data
items.text: A dataset enters the workspace through File ▸ Import Dataset… or the Import button above the workspace tree. TSE Analytics reads three kinds of files: the .tse export of the PhenoMaster software, the IntelliCage export (.zip) and the IntelliMaze export (.zip).

items.title: Exporting from PhenoMaster
items.text:
TSE Analytics reads the export the PhenoMaster software writes for it, not the raw recordings:

  1. In PhenoMaster, open the Export menu and choose TSE Analytics.
  2. Select the data to export. Besides the main data you can add the ActiMot raw data (Act.raw), the calorimetry bins (Calo.bin) and the DrinkFeed bins (DFT.bin); with a licensed BodyWeight module the DrinkFeed file also holds the body weights.
  3. Click Start Export, keep or change the proposed name — Export, the project id, the date and the time, with the extension .tse — and click Save. A message confirms the finished export.

items.title: Importing a PhenoMaster export
items.text:
1. Choose File ▸ Import Dataset… and select the .tse file.

  2. Choose the optional tables to import. Only the tables the file contains can be ticked.

    • Calo bin data — the calorimetry bins, for the Calo viewer.
    • DrinkFeed bin data and DrinkFeed raw data — for the DrinkFeed viewer.
    • ActiMot raw data — for the ActiMot viewer.
    • Group Housing data — for the Group Housing viewer.

  3. Click Import. The import runs in the background; a message shows its progress, and the dataset appears in the tree when it is done.

Tip

Large exports take longer to import and use more memory. Tick only the tables you need; you can import an export again with other tables later.

During the import the dataset's metadata is extracted: the animals with their properties (box, weight, …), the variables with their units and default aggregation, the sample interval and the recording period. Look at them in the Info, Animals and Factors tabs of the sidebar.

items.title: Importing an IntelliCage or IntelliMaze export
items.text: Choose File ▸ Import Dataset… and select the .zip file. There are no options; the import creates the dataset with the tables the export holds — for IntelliCage the Visits and Nosepokes tables, for IntelliMaze one raw table per module. See IntelliCage and IntelliMaze.

items.title: Several datasets in one workspace
items.text:
Import as many datasets as you like, one after the other; each keeps its own animals, factors, variables and settings. The menus and the toolbox act on the dataset (or datatable) that is selected in the tree. Datasets of the same design can be merged into one; see Merging datasets.

Note

CSV files and the import of extension data from CSV are internal features (Settings ▸ General ▸ Enable internal features). With them on, the file picker also accepts .csv and the dataset's context menu offers Import calo data…, Import drink/feed data…, Import ActiMot data… and Import group housing data….

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Workspaces
  • Data table

items.title: File
items.text:
• New Workspace (Ctrl+N): start with an empty workspace. If the current one has unsaved changes, you are asked first.
  • Open Workspace… (Ctrl+O): open a .workspace or .duckdb file.
  • Open Recent: the workspaces you opened or saved last.
  • Save Workspace (Ctrl+S) and Save Workspace As… (Ctrl+Shift+S): see Workspaces.
  • Import Dataset…: add a PhenoMaster, IntelliCage or IntelliMaze export to the workspace; see Importing data.
  • Export Merged CSV…: only shown while an IntelliMaze dataset is selected; see IntelliMaze.
  • Settings…: the Settings dialog.
  • Quit (Ctrl+Q): close the application; unsaved changes are asked about.

items.title: View
items.text:
• Toggle Sidebar hides or shows the workspace tree and the dataset details.
  • Toggle Log hides or shows the log pane.
  • Zoom In (Ctrl++), Zoom Out (Ctrl+-) and Reset Zoom (Ctrl+0) scale the whole window, like a web browser: from 50 % to 300 % in the usual steps (…, 90, 100, 110, 125, 150 %, …). A short message shows the new size, and the application starts with the same zoom next time.

Tip

The zoom keys work wherever the focus is, in a report as well. Ctrl+= zooms in too, and the keypad's +, - and 0 count as well.

items.title: Toolbox
items.text: The Toolbox menu opens an analysis for the selected datatable; it is disabled until you select one in the tree. Each category is a submenu; a tool that does not apply to the selected data (an IntelliCage analysis on a PhenoMaster dataset, for example) is greyed out. The Toolbox chapter describes every tool.

items.title: Assistant and Pipeline
items.text: These menus appear when Settings ▸ General ▸ Enable internal features is on. Assistant ▸ Open TSE Assistant opens the chat panel (AI assistance); Pipeline creates, opens and imports pipelines for the selected dataset (Pipelines).

items.title: Help
items.text:
• Documentation opens this manual — the copy that ships with the application, or the online version when Settings ▸ General ▸ Help mode is Use online help.
  • About shows the version, the licence and the third-party libraries.

items.title: Keyboard shortcuts
items.text:
Keys Where What Ctrl+O anywhere Open a workspace Ctrl+S anywhere Save the workspace Ctrl+S in a report Save the report Ctrl+Shift+S anywhere Save the workspace as… Ctrl+N anywhere New workspace Ctrl+Q anywhere Quit Ctrl++ (or Ctrl+=) anywhere Zoom in Ctrl+- anywhere Zoom out Ctrl+0 anywhere Reset the zoom to 100 % Enter on a tree row Open the selected datatable, report or pipeline → / ← on a tree row Expand / collapse the row Middle-click on a panel tab Close the panel Enter / Shift+Enter in the assistant Send / new line

Note

The full Reference ▸ Keyboard shortcuts page lists the shortcuts of the report editor as well.

items.title: Workspaces
items.text:
A workspace is the file that holds your study: every dataset you imported or merged, the datatables you derived, the animals, factors and outlier settings you edited, and the reports and pipelines of every dataset. Open it again and everything is back.

Not part of the workspace: the panels that were open, the settings of the analysis tools (the application remembers those per tool, on your computer), the theme and the layout of the window.

items.title: New, open, save
items.text:
• File ▸ New Workspace starts an empty workspace.
  • File ▸ Open Workspace… (Ctrl+O) opens a .workspace or .duckdb file. On the desktop you can also double-click the file, or drop it on the application icon; a second start of the application hands the file to the window that is already running.

  • File ▸ Open Recent lists the workspaces you used last.

  • File ▸ Save Workspace (Ctrl+S) writes the file; the first save asks for a name. File ▸ Save Workspace As… (Ctrl+Shift+S) writes a copy under a new name — and a new format, if you change the extension.

The window title and the status bar show the file name; a • next to it means there are unsaved changes.

items.title: Two file formats
items.text:
Extension Format When to use it .workspace The standard format (a Python pickle). The default; fast to save and to open. .duckdb A DuckDB database. When other tools should read the data, or for very large workspaces.

The extension you give the file decides the format. Both hold the same content.

Warning

Open only workspace files you trust. Opening a .workspace file runs code stored in it, like opening a document with macros.

items.title: Unsaved changes
items.text:
Workspaces are not saved automatically. When you quit, start a new workspace or open another one while the current one has unsaved changes, the application asks:

Save writes the workspace first, Don't Save discards the changes, Cancel keeps the window open. Closing the window asks the same question.

Tip

Analysis results are not stored in the workspace — the reports are. Add the results you want to keep to a report before you save (see Reports).

items.text:
• Importing data
  • Workspace tree

items.title: IntelliCage and IntelliMaze
items.text: Besides PhenoMaster, TSE Analytics reads the exports of two behavioural systems. Both come as a .zip file and import through File ▸ Import Dataset… without options; the workspace, the tree, the factors, the data table and most of the toolbox work the same as for PhenoMaster data.

items.title: IntelliCage
items.text: An IntelliCage export becomes a dataset with two datatables, Visits and Nosepokes, and the raw tables of the export (Visits, Nosepokes, Environment, HardwareEvents, Log) under Raw Data. The animals with the groups the experiment defined (for example Sex and Group) become factors. See Visits and nosepokes for the tables and the three IntelliCage analyses of the toolbox.

items.title: IntelliMaze
items.text: An IntelliMaze export becomes a dataset with one datatable per module — AnimalGate, ConsumptionScale, RunningWheel, Actor, OperantDevice, IntelliCage, whichever the export holds — a combined Main table, and the raw registrations of every module under Raw Data. See IntelliMaze, including the merged CSV export that other IntelliMaze tools read.

items.title: IntelliMaze
items.text: An IntelliMaze experiment combines several modules around an animal gate. The import creates one datatable per module and a Main table that joins them, so the animals' passages, consumption, running and operant registrations can be analysed together and separately.

items.title: The datatables
items.text:
Module Datatable Variables AnimalGate AnimalGate the duration of the passage and the weight measured in the gate ConsumptionScale ConsumptionScale the consumption RunningWheel RunningWheel left and right revolutions Actor Actor the mode and state of the actor OperantDevice, IntelliCage their own tables when the export holds them — Main all of the above, by time

The raw registrations of every module (sessions, antenna readings, logs, the module's variables) sit under Raw Data. The animals and the groups of the experiment (Group, Sex, Strain, Treatment, …) become the dataset's animals and factors.

items.title: Merged CSV export
items.text:
File ▸ Export Merged CSV… — shown while an IntelliMaze dataset is selected — writes the raw tables of the chosen modules into one CSV file ordered by time, in the format other IntelliMaze tools read.

  • Tick the extensions (modules) to include.
  • Delimiter — semicolon, comma or tab.
  • Format — New Format or Old Format, for the tool that will read the file.
  • Export Registrations and Export Variables — which parts of each module go into the file.

The export runs in the background and can be cancelled; the file downloads when it is done.

items.title: Visits and nosepokes
items.text: The IntelliCage records every visit of an animal to one of the four corners and every nosepoke at a door inside a corner, with the licks at the bottle behind it.

items.title: The datatables
items.text:
• Visits — one row per visit: the animal, the corner, the start, the duration, the number and duration of the nosepokes and licks during the visit, whether the corner was the correct one (PlaceError, SideErrors, ConditionErrors), the illumination and the temperature.
  • Nosepokes — one row per nosepoke: the animal, the visit, the side, the duration, the licks, and the errors.

Both are ordinary datatables: open them, filter them, derive resampled copies, and analyse them with any tool that takes a variable — a histogram of the visit duration per group, a mixed-design ANOVA of the licks by group and day.

items.title: The IntelliCage tools
items.text:
Three tools of the Toolbox are made for these tables and appear only for IntelliCage and IntelliMaze datasets:

  • Transitions — does the animal move between the corners in a pattern?
  • Place Preference — does it prefer the correct corner?
  • Learning Curve — does its performance improve over the experiment?

Select the Visits datatable before opening the first two.

items.title: Pipelines
items.text:
A pipeline is an analysis you can run again: a graph of nodes that starts from a datatable, transforms it, runs tools on it, branches on their results and writes them into a report. Build it once for one dataset, run it after every import, or export it and import it into another workspace — or let an AI assistant build it for you from a published method.

Note

Pipelines are an internal feature: turn on Settings ▸ General ▸ Enable internal features to see the Pipeline menu and the Pipelines rows in the tree.

items.title: Creating and opening
items.text:
• Pipeline ▸ New Pipeline… (or New Pipeline… in a dataset's context menu) asks for a name and opens an empty editor. A pipeline belongs to the dataset that is selected.
  • Pipeline ▸ Open ▸ lists the pipelines of the selected dataset; the tree's Pipelines rows open them too.
  • Pipeline ▸ Import Pipeline… reads a pipeline exported as JSON into the selected dataset.

items.title: The editor
items.text:
• The node palette on the left lists the nodes by category; Search nodes… filters it. Drag a node onto the canvas.
  • The canvas shows the nodes and their connections. Drag from an output port to an input port to connect them; select a node to edit it; Delete removes it.
  • The properties on the right are the settings of the selected node — the same form the tool has in the toolbox.
  • The results below the canvas show the last run (see Running a pipeline).
  • The toolbar: Save (the name gets a * while there are unsaved changes), Run / Cancel, Undo, Redo, Fit view, Export (as JSON), Import and Description.

items.title: Description
items.text: Description opens a dialog for what the pipeline does and where it comes from — the paper whose method it implements, say. The first line shows under the toolbar; click it to edit. The description is saved on its own: the canvas keeps its unsaved changes. It travels with the pipeline when you export and import it.

items.title: Built by an AI assistant
items.text:
An assistant — the TSE Assistant, or Claude Code and Claude Desktop through the MCP server — can build a pipeline for you: Implement the workflow described in \<a paper> in a new pipeline. It chooses the nodes, checks the whole graph before saving it, and lays the nodes out as a tree, left to right; the node captions name the method's steps and the description cites the source. Replacing a pipeline you already have asks you first; if the pipeline is open in the editor, its unsaved changes are replaced when you agree. The assistant needs Allow AI assistants to change the workspace in the AI permissions. Example: the 39 steps shows such a pipeline.

An assistant also turns a conversation into a pipeline, so its results can be run again later: ask the TSE Assistant Save the pipeline that reproduces the current chat, or press Save as Pipeline in the header of its panel. The analysis tools it ran become tool nodes with the same settings, the Python code it wrote becomes Python nodes, and a datatable it derived becomes the Datatable node that names it. Changes it made to the workspace — factors, outlier settings, animal properties — are not nodes, so the description names what the pipeline relies on. Every Python node starts with fresh variables: the assistant merges the code a result needs into one node, and a pipeline whose code reads a variable an earlier chat run left behind is refused until it does. The assistant then runs the pipeline to compare its results with the conversation. While Run Python code is Off, an assistant cannot save Python nodes.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Nodes — what each node does
  • Running a pipeline
  • Example: the 39 steps

items.title: Example: the 39 steps
items.text:
Speakman, Fletcher & Vaanholt (2013) describe how to analyse energy intake and expenditure so that differences in body size do not pass for effects of a treatment: The '39 steps': an algorithm for performing statistical analysis of data on energy intake and expenditure (Disease Models & Mechanisms 6:293–301, open access on PubMed Central). This page walks through the pipeline that implements its core — the one an AI assistant builds when you ask it to implement the paper.

Note

Pipelines are an internal feature: turn on Settings ▸ General ▸ Enable internal features.

items.title: The graph
items.text:
1. Datatable — Main, the calorimetry data.
  2. Per-animal Summary — one row per animal: the paper's first rule is that each animal appears once.
  3. Add Variable — BodyMass from the animal property Weight, the body mass entered in PhenoMaster. The energy expenditure is not divided by it: the ANCOVA corrects for body size.
  4. Normality of EE — step 1.
  5. Normal ▸ ANCOVA — EE by Treatment with the covariate BodyMass, Slopes: Test, drop if not significant — steps 22–31. Its first paragraph names the step of the paper the result matches.
  6. Decision — interaction_kept = 1: do the slopes differ between the groups (step 30)? Yes ▸ Regression of EE on BodyMass per group shows the slope of each group (step 31).
  7. Not normal ▸ Transformation — Box-Cox fitted within Treatment (step 3), then Normality again: normal, an ANCOVA of the transformed EE; still not normal, the Non-parametric Tests (steps 15–21).
  8. Report nodes, set to Replace it (once per run), collect the results in one report, 39 steps: EE.

items.title: Reading the run
items.text: In the figure, EE passed the normality test, so the ANCOVA ran and the Box-Cox branch was skipped (Not taken: …). The ANCOVA kept the treatment × body mass interaction (p_interaction = 0.045): the treatment changes how energy expenditure grows with body mass — step 30 — so the Decision node sent the data to Yes, and the regression shows the slope of each treatment. The ANCOVA report adds the Johnson–Neyman ranges: the body masses at which the treatments differ.

items.title: With lean and fat mass
items.text: With body composition from an EchoMRI or DXA scan, store lean and fat mass as animal properties — in the Animals tab, or let an assistant set them — add an Add Variable node for each, and set the ANCOVA's Covariates to Two covariates (steps 32–36).

items.title: What the pipeline leaves out
items.text:
• The whole-animal comparison without body-size correction (steps 5–14): add a One-way ANOVA or N-way ANOVA node on the per-animal data.
  • Organ masses as covariates (steps 37–38): a correlation matrix and principal component scores as predictors are not part of it.
  • Power (step 11): when the treatment is not significant, the ANCOVA reports the smallest effect the design could detect.

The paper ends with step 39: consult a statistician before publishing results.
