items.title: Nodes
items.text: A pipeline is built from a few core nodes and from every analysis tool of the toolbox.

items.title: Core nodes
items.text: Node Category What it does Datatable Input The datatable the pipeline starts from — choose it in the properties. Datatable Output Output Stores the incoming datatable as a datatable of the dataset. Report Output Writes the incoming result into a report of the dataset. Resample Transform Aggregates the rows into wider time bins, each variable with its aggregation. Transformation Transform Adds a transformed copy of one variable as a new column: Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, Log or Log10. Descriptive Statistics Transform Reports the count, mean, spread and quartiles of every numeric column; the datatable passes on unchanged. Per-animal Summary Transform Collapses the data to one row per animal — or per animal and level of a within-subject factor. Add Variable Transform Adds a variable: an animal property such as the body mass, an expression, a running sum or a difference. Normality Control Tests a variable for normality and routes the datatable to the Normal or the Not normal output, so the graph can branch. Checkbox Control A switch with a True and a False output, to turn a branch on or off without rebuilding the graph. Decision Control Compares a statistic of the analysis before it with a threshold and routes to Yes or No. Python Code Runs Python code on the datatable — a figure, a table or a number the toolbox does not offer, such as the code an AI assistant wrote in a chat.

items.title: Report
items.text:
• Report name — the report of the dataset the result goes to.
  • If the report exists — Append to it, or Replace it (once per run): the run's first write to the report starts it afresh and every later one appends, so a pipeline can run again without doubling its report. Several Report nodes may write to the same report.

A Datatable Output node fails when the dataset already has a datatable of its name — rename or delete that datatable before the pipeline runs again.

items.title: Transformation
items.text:
• Variable and New column — the variable to transform and the name of the column it goes to; the new column is a variable the nodes downstream can choose.
  • Method — Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, Log or Log10. Box-Cox and the logarithms need positive values; missing values stay missing.
  • Fit λ (Box-Cox and Yeo-Johnson) — To the pooled values, or Within groups (variable ~ factor) with the Groups factor, a between-subject factor other than Animal and Total: the λ that makes the residuals of the group model most normal, as R's MASS::boxcox does on the group model — what an analysis of the groups assumes. The report shows λ and how it was fitted.

items.title: Per-animal Summary
items.text:
Most statistics of whole animals count each animal once. This node turns a time series into one row per animal:

  • Split by — within-subject factors, such as LightCycle, for one row per animal and level; leave it empty for one row per animal.
  • Aggregation — Each variable's own (its mean, sum … as the variable says), or one for all: Mean, Median, Sum, Minimum, Maximum — the mean of daily sums after a Resample to one day, for example.

Removed outliers are left out first. The between-subject factors (a genotype, a treatment) come along; the result has no time axis. The report previews the values of up to 50 rows and 20 variables.

items.title: Add Variable
items.text:
• New variable — its name.
  • From — Animal property (choose the Animal property), Expression (over the datatable's columns, such as EE * 24 or Feed / Weight), Cumulative sum or Difference to the previous value (of a Variable, per animal).
  • Unit and Aggregation — how the new variable combines per animal or per time bin.

An animal property becomes a covariate this way: the body mass, lean and fat mass. Every animal needs the property, as a number; an empty value becomes a missing value. The node reads the properties each time the pipeline runs.

items.title: Normality
items.text:
• Variable, Method (Shapiro-Wilk, D'Agostino-Pearson, Anderson-Darling, Kolmogorov-Smirnov) and Alpha: the datatable goes to Normal when the p-value is above alpha, else to Not normal.

The test uses the rows that reach it — after a Per-animal Summary, one value per animal — and leaves removed outliers out.

items.title: Decision
items.text:
A Decision node follows an analysis node, or another Decision node on the same analysis, and routes on one of the statistics the analysis publishes:

  • Statistic — the node offers what the analysis before it publishes:
    • One-way ANOVA: p (the factor), p_levene (Levene's test), welch (1 when Welch's ANOVA ran).
    • ANCOVA: p_factor, p_covariate, p_covariate_2, p_interaction (the test of the slopes), interaction_kept (1 when the slopes differ between the groups), step (the step of the 39 steps the outcome matches) and p_residual_normality.
    • Non-parametric Tests: p.
    • Python: the keys listed in its Published statistics.
  • Condition (<, ≤, >, ≥, =, ≠) and Threshold (0.05 by default): when the condition holds the datatable goes to Yes, else to No.

A statistic that does not apply to a run — the second covariate's p-value with one covariate, say — fails the node with the list of what the analysis did publish.

items.title: Python
items.text:
The Python node runs Python code on the datatable reaching it, in the guarded Python process an AI assistant's code runs in (see Running Python code) — for a figure, a table or a number the toolbox does not offer. It is how a pipeline keeps the code an assistant wrote in a chat (Built by an AI assistant).

Every Python node starts with fresh variables, so its code must stand on its own. The code sees:

  • df — the datatable reaching the node, as a pandas table, with removed outliers left empty, as the app shows them;
  • dfs — that datatable and the More datatables by name; meta — their units, factors and sampling interval, the colour of each factor level (meta["Main"]["factors"]["Animal"]["colors"] for the animals, the colours to plot with) and the animals' properties (meta["Main"]["animals"]["1001"]["Text1"], say), read afresh at every run, so a figure follows a colour you change later;
  • pd, np, plt, sns and mpl — pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and seaborn;
  • keep_table(table, name) — keeps a table, which the results pane offers for download or as a new datatable;
  • publish(key, value) — publishes a number a Decision node after this one can route on.

What the code prints, its result, the tables it keeps and the figures it draws (as images, at most eight) make up the node's report. The node has two outputs:

  • Result — the datatable, passed on unchanged, with the report: connect a Report or a Decision node.
  • Table — the table the code assigns to result (result = means), as a new datatable for the nodes after it. When the code sets no table there, those nodes are skipped: No table: the code set no DataFrame as result.

The settings:

  • Code — shown with colours. Edit… opens it in a wide editor: Tab indents, Shift+Tab leaves the editor, Ctrl+Enter applies; Apply keeps the change, Cancel drops it.
  • More datatables — other datatables of the dataset, which the code reads as dfs["<name>"].
  • Table variables — the variables of the table the code sets as result, separated by commas. Nothing has run when you connect the nodes after Table, so these are the variables their settings offer.
  • Published statistics — the keys the code passes to publish, separated by commas: the statistics a Decision node after this one offers.

Note

A Python node runs only while Settings ▸ AI permissions ▸ Run Python code is not Off; otherwise it fails with a message saying so. A run you start in the editor never asks; a run an assistant starts shows you the code first when the setting is Ask before each run.

A run starts one Python process for all its Python nodes and ends it with the run. A failing node shows the Python error and what the code printed before it, and the nodes after it are skipped. Code that draws random numbers — jittered points, bootstrapped error bars — gives slightly different figures on every run.

items.title: Tool nodes
items.text: Every tool of the Toolbox is a node in its category, with the same settings. A tool node takes a datatable and produces a result — the report of the tool — that a Report node stores; it passes the datatable on as well, so a Decision or another node can follow it. A tool that does not apply to the dataset (an IntelliCage analysis on a PhenoMaster dataset) is not offered.

items.title: Connections
items.text: An output feeds as many nodes as you connect; an input takes one connection, and the editor refuses a connection that would close a loop. A node with an unconnected input is skipped when the pipeline runs, and everything downstream of it too.

items.title: Running a pipeline
items.text:
Run executes the graph in the background — the unsaved state of the canvas, so you can try changes before saving — and reports on every node.

The results pane lists the nodes with their state and shows, for the selected node, its report, its warnings and its Results menu with the downloadable tables. A message summarises the run: Pipeline finished: N nodes., or how many failed.

  • Done — the node ran. An analysis that publishes statistics (ANCOVA, One-way ANOVA, Non-parametric Tests, or a Python node that called publish) shows them above its report — Statistics: p_factor = 0.04264, … — the numbers a Decision node routes on.
  • Skipped — the node did not run; its message (select the node, or hover it) says why: a branch a control node did not take (Not taken: EE looks normal (Shapiro-Wilk p = 0.732, alpha = 0.05) — every node further down that branch shows the same reason), an input that is not connected, or a node before it that failed.
  • Failed — with the error (a Python node shows the Python error and what its code printed before it); the rest of the run goes on.

Report nodes write into the dataset's reports as the run proceeds — appending, or starting the report afresh when set to Replace it (once per run) — and Datatable Output nodes add datatables to the dataset; the tree updates when the run is done. Cancel stops a run after the current node; a Python node's code is stopped at once.

items.title: Export and import
items.text:
Export writes the pipeline as a JSON file, with its description; Pipeline ▸ Import Pipeline… (or Import in the editor) reads it into the selected dataset, under its stored name or one you choose when the name is taken. The graph refers to datatables and variables by name, so it runs on any dataset with the same names.

A pipeline with Python nodes carries their code. It runs only while Settings ▸ AI permissions ▸ Run Python code is not Off: a run you start in the editor does not ask, and a run an assistant starts shows you the code first when the setting is Ask before each run. Import pipelines with Python code only from people you trust.

items.title: About and licences
items.text:
Help ▸ About shows the version of TSE Analytics you are running, with two tabs:

  • About — the copyright and the licence of TSE Analytics, and a link to the source repository. TSE Analytics is proprietary software of TSE Systems, which may be used, copied or distributed only under a written licence agreement with TSE Systems.
  • Third-party libraries — every open-source library the application is built with, for the analysis engine, the user interface, the bundled fonts and the desktop window, each with a link to its home. The licence texts of the analysis engine's libraries ship with the application in THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt, next to the server program (in the installation folder, under resources/server/); those of the desktop window in LICENSE.electron.txt and LICENSES.chromium.html, at the top of the installation folder.

When you report a problem to TSE Service, include the version shown here.

items.title: The log pane
items.text:
View ▸ Toggle Log shows the application's log below the panels: imports and their durations, the analyses that ran, and every warning and error, newest at the bottom.

  • The level select hides messages below the chosen level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR).
  • Clear empties the pane; × hides it.

items.title: The log file
items.text:
Everything the pane shows, and more, goes to a log file that TSE Service may ask for:

Operating system Folder Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\TSE Systems\tse-analytics\Logs Linux ~/.local/state/tse-analytics/log

The start-up page's Open log folder button opens it when the analysis engine failed to start.

items.title: When something goes wrong
items.text:
• An import fails or takes very long. Import only the tables you need; the ActiMot raw table of a long recording needs several gigabytes of memory. Check the log for the message.
  • An analysis fails. The tool panel shows the error next to its toolbar and the log has the details. The usual causes: a factor with one level, a variable that is all missing, too few animals for the test.
  • The window says Session ended or Stopped. The analysis engine stopped; close the window and start the application again. Unsaved changes are lost, so save the workspace often.
  • A workspace does not open. It was saved by a newer version, or the file is damaged. The log names the reason.
  • The engine does not start. The start-up page offers Restart, Open log folder and Quit; the log file has the error. A firewall that blocks local connections, or another program on the same port, are common causes.

items.title: Reports
items.text: A report is a document of a dataset: the results you collect from the analyses, with your own text around them. Reports live under the dataset in the tree, are saved in the workspace, and export to HTML or print to PDF.

items.title: Adding results
items.text:
Every source of results has an Add Report button: the analysis tools, the data table's Descriptive Statistics, the Fast Line Plot (a snapshot of the chart), the TSE Assistant (the conversation) and the report node of a pipeline. It asks for a report name; a new name creates a report, an existing one appends to it.

A result arrives as a block you edit around: the block itself — the header with the settings, the figures and the tables — is fixed, so it stays a faithful record of the analysis. Write your interpretation above or below it, delete the block if you no longer need it.

items.title: The editor
items.text:
The editor toolbar offers undo and redo, the block type (paragraph, headings 1 to 4), bold, italic, underline and strikethrough, bullet and numbered lists, a quote, a code block, a horizontal rule and a 3 × 3 table. Links are recognised as you type them. Images pasted into the report are stored in it.

The panel toolbar:

  • Save (Ctrl+S) — the report is also saved automatically shortly after you stop typing; the status next to the buttons says Saving…, Unsaved changes or Saved with the time.
  • Export HTML — a standalone HTML file that opens in any browser, figures included.
  • Print — the system print dialog; choose Print to PDF (Microsoft Print to PDF on Windows) for a PDF file.
  • Reload — appears when the report changed on the server (an assistant added to it, for example): reload to take the changes, or save to overwrite them.

items.title: Managing reports
items.text: In the tree, a report's context menu offers Open, Rename…, Clone… and Delete. Reports are part of the workspace file; save the workspace to keep them.

items.title: Toolbox
items.text: The Toolbox menu holds the analyses. Select a datatable in the tree, pick a tool from its category, and the tool opens as a panel: the settings on the right, the result on the left.

items.title: How a tool panel works
items.text:
1. Choose the settings in the sidebar on the right. Every tool names the variable or variables it analyses and, for most, a Group by: Animal (one series or one test group per animal), a factor of the dataset (one per level), or Total (everything pooled). The analyses of the ANOVA category take factors instead — the groups or conditions they compare, never Animal or Total (Common settings). Fields that do not apply to the current choice are hidden.
  2. Update runs the analysis in the background; the report replaces the empty panel when it is done. Cancel stops a long run. The settings are remembered per tool, so the next panel of the same tool starts where you left off.
  3. Read the report: the header names the dataset, the datatable, the settings and the data used (animals, rows, outlier settings, sample interval), then come the figures and tables.
  4. Keep the result: Add Report appends the report to a report of the dataset (you choose or create the report by name); Results ▾ downloads the result tables.
  • Download Excel — every result table of the run in one workbook, one sheet per table.
  • Download CSV — one table.
  • Add as Datatable… — a result table becomes a datatable of the dataset, for further analysis.

The tool reads the whole datatable with the dataset's outlier settings applied; the filter and the column choice of an open data table do not affect it. Every animal of the datatable takes part — derive a datatable without the animals you want to leave out (Deriving a datatable).

items.title: Common settings
items.text:
• Factor, Factors, Between-subject factor, Within-subject factor(s) (the ANOVA category): the factors whose levels the analysis compares — a between-subject factor such as the genotype or the treatment, a within-subject factor such as the light cycle, as the label says. Animal and Total are not offered: each level of Animal is a single animal and Total has one level, so there is nothing to compare. A dataset without a factor of its own leaves the list empty and says so under it — add one with Edit Factors in the Factors tab (see Factors).
  • Effect size (the ANOVA family): no effect size, unbiased Cohen d, Hedges g, eta-square, odds ratio, area under the curve, or common language effect size, reported with every pairwise comparison in a column named after it (cohen, hedges, eta_square, odds_ratio, AUC, CLES). No effect size adds no column.
  • P-value adjustment (N-way, repeated measures, mixed-design ANOVA and ANCOVA): none, one-step Bonferroni, one-step Sidak, step-down Bonferroni, Benjamini/Hochberg FDR or Benjamini/Yekutieli FDR, applied to the pairwise comparisons of each contrast; the tables then add p_corr (the adjusted p-value) and p_adjust (the method).
  • Pairwise tests (repeated measures and mixed-design ANOVA): untick to skip the post-hoc comparisons, which grow with the square of the number of levels.

items.title: ANCOVA
items.text: Analysis of covariance tests whether groups differ in a variable once one or two continuous covariates are held constant — whether treated animals eat less than controls for their body weight, or burn more energy for their lean and fat mass. It combines an ANOVA with a regression on the covariates, and follows the procedure of Speakman, Fletcher & Vaanholt (2013), The '39 steps': an algorithm for performing statistical analysis of data on energy intake and expenditure (Disease Models & Mechanisms 6:293–301): it first tests whether the covariate's slope differs between the groups, drops that test when it is not significant, and reports which step of the paper's algorithm the result corresponds to.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable to test, such as energy expenditure or food intake. Do not divide it by body mass first: the analysis corrects for body size itself.
  • Covariates — One covariate (body mass, say) or Two covariates (e.g. lean and fat mass).
  • Covariate and Second covariate — the continuous variables to adjust for; they must differ from each other and from the dependent variable. An animal property such as the weight becomes a variable through Add Variable.
  • Factor — the between-subject factor (genotype, treatment).
  • Slopes — whether a covariate's slope may differ between the groups:
    • Test, drop if not significant (the paper's procedure) — the model starts with every group × covariate interaction (with two covariates also their interaction) and drops the non-significant ones, the least significant first.
    • Always include — keeps every interaction.
    • Assume parallel — the classic ANCOVA, without interactions.
  • Alpha — the significance level of every decision (0.05, 0.1 or 0.01).
  • P-value adjustment — for the pairwise comparisons: Tukey-Kramer (the default) or one of the corrections of the other ANOVAs.

The analysis uses one value per animal: each variable aggregated over the animal's rows with its aggregation. For animals measured under several conditions, use the Linear Mixed Model — the paper's "individual as a random factor".

items.title: Result
items.text:
• Outcome — one paragraph first: which effects are significant and the step of the paper that applies — for example step 26 (the groups differ independently of body mass), step 25 (the difference is due to body size), step 28 (both matter, the slopes are parallel), step 30 (the slopes differ) or, with two covariates, steps 33–36. It also names the interactions that were dropped.
  • Covariates by group — whether the groups differ in each covariate (one-way ANOVA) and its mean per group.
  • Full model (type III) — every term with SS, DF, MS, F, p_unc and np2 (partial eta-square), before any interaction is dropped. The tests are type III on sum-to-zero coded factors, as SPSS, Minitab and R compute them.
  • Final model (type III) — the same columns after the non-significant interactions are dropped, with R² and adjusted R². While a group × covariate interaction stays in the model, the factor's row tests the groups where the covariate is 0; compare the groups with the adjusted means and the Johnson–Neyman ranges instead.
  • Slopes — the change in the dependent variable per unit of each covariate, per group when its slope differs.
  • Adjusted means — each group's mean predicted at the covariates' overall means, with its standard error and 95 % interval, next to the raw mean.
  • Pairwise comparisons of the adjusted means — for each pair of groups A and B: diff (A − B), se, T, p_unc, the adjusted p-value (p_tukey, or p_corr) and d (the difference over the residual standard deviation).
  • Johnson–Neyman regions of significance — with one covariate whose slope differs between the groups: the covariate values at which two groups differ significantly.
  • Model checks — Shapiro–Wilk of the residuals and the Brown–Forsythe test of their variances across the groups. With two covariates, their correlation and variance inflation factor: the analysis assumes independent covariates.
  • Sensitivity — when the factor is not significant: the smallest group effect this design would detect with 80 % power (step 11 of the paper).
  • The figure — the data against each covariate with the final model's fitted line per group; diamonds mark the adjusted means. With two covariates, one panel per covariate, the points adjusted to the other covariate's mean.

In a pipeline, an ANCOVA node also publishes its result as numbers — p_factor, p_covariate, p_interaction, interaction_kept, step and more — that a Decision node routes on; Example: the 39 steps builds the paper's procedure around it.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text:
The paper's own example: the metabolism of 15 animals in three treatment levels, with body mass as the covariate.

  1. Slopes. The full model's Levels × Body mass interaction has p = 0.31: the slopes do not differ, so it is dropped.
  2. Final model. Levels is significant (F = 45.96, p < 0.001); body mass only shows a trend (p = 0.063).
  3. Outcome. Step 26: the treatment levels differ in metabolism independently of body mass. The pairwise comparisons of the adjusted means show that every level differs from the others.

items.title: Linear Mixed Model
items.text: A linear mixed model tests whether a between-subject factor shifts a repeatedly measured variable, with a random intercept per animal that absorbs the animal's own level, and a covariate that can vary from measurement to measurement. It is the flexible alternative to the mixed-design ANOVA when the design is unbalanced, has missing measurements, or needs a time-varying covariate.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable to model.
  • Covariate handling — how the covariate enters the model:
    • Time-varying (total effect) — the covariate's within-animal deviation is adjusted for; the group estimate is the total effect of the factor.
    • Between + within (direct effect) — separate slopes for the between-animal and the within-animal part of the covariate; the group estimate is the direct effect, net of the covariate.
    • Baseline (first within level) — each animal's covariate is held at its value in the first within-subject level.
    • None (no covariate).
  • Covariate — the variable, shown for the first three options.
  • Between-subject factor and Within-subject factor.
  • Alpha — the significance level (0.05, 0.1 or 0.01).
  • Bootstrap — Off, 200 or 1000 parametric bootstrap replicates per tested term, for confidence intervals that do not rely on the normal approximation; slow (about 36 ms per replicate and term).
  • Leave-one-out — refit the model with each animal left out, to show how much any single animal drives the result.
  • Seed — the random seed of the bootstrap.

items.title: Result
items.text: The model summary with the fixed effects (the factor levels, the within-subject levels, the covariate and the interaction) — estimate, standard error, z, p-value and confidence interval — the random-intercept variance, the tests of the terms, and, when enabled, the bootstrap intervals and the leave-one-out table. A term whose confidence interval excludes zero is significant at the chosen alpha. A plot of the random intercepts shows each animal's in its colour, sorted, with its interval: an animal far from the others stands out.

items.title: Mixed-design ANOVA
items.text: Mixed-design ANOVA combines one between-subject factor (genotype, treatment) with one within-subject factor (days, light cycle, intervals) and tests both main effects and their interaction — does the treatment change how the variable develops over time?

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable to test.
  • Between-subject factor and Within-subject factor — one each (see Factors for the roles).
  • Pairwise tests, Effect size, P-value adjustment — as for the repeated measures ANOVA.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• Sphericity test for the within-subject factor.
  • Mixed-design ANOVA: rows for the between-subject factor, the within-subject factor and their Interaction, with SS, DF1, DF2, MS, F, p_unc, np2 (partial eta-square) and eps (the Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon of the within-subject factor). When the sphericity test fails, the within-subject row adds p_GG_corr (the corrected p-value) and sphericity, W_spher and p_spher.
  • Pairwise post-hoc tests: the within-subject levels compared over all animals (paired), the between-subject levels compared on each animal's mean over the within-subject levels, then the between-subject levels compared within every level of the within-subject factor.

Only animals with a value in every level of the within-subject factor take part.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text:
RER of WT and KO animals across time bins:

  1. Sphericity holds (p not significant).
  2. ANOVA. Genotype p = 0.719 — no overall difference between WT and KO. Time bin p < 0.00001 — RER differs across bins, with a very large effect size. Interaction p = 0.527 — the temporal profile does not differ between the genotypes.
  3. Post-hoc. Some bins differ from each other (bin 0 versus 2, p < 0.05), while WT and KO do not differ within any bin.

RER changes over the day in both genotypes in the same way; there is no genotype effect and no interaction.

items.title: N-way ANOVA
items.text: N-way ANOVA tests the effects of two or more between-subject factors — and their interactions — on a variable: a two-way ANOVA for genotype and treatment, a three-way ANOVA with sex added, and so on.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable whose means are compared.
  • Factors — tick two or more between-subject factors (not Animal or Total, see Common settings).
  • Effect size and P-value adjustment — for the pairwise comparisons (see Toolbox).

items.title: Result
items.text:
• Two-way ANOVA (Three-way, Multi-way with more factors): one row per factor and per interaction (Treatment * Sex) with SS, DF, MS, F, p_unc and np2, plus the Residual row. The sums of squares are type II. The p_unc cells are shaded from white (p = 0) to red (p = 1).
  • Pairwise post-hoc tests (two factors only): for each Contrast — the first factor, the second, then their interaction, which compares the levels of the second factor within each level of the first (named in the column after the first factor; "-" on the other rows) — and each pair A/B: mean_A, std_A, mean_B, std_B, Paired, Parametric, T, dof, alternative, p_unc, with an adjustment p_corr (adjusted within each contrast) and p_adjust (the method), then BF10 (the Bayes factor) and the effect size. A contrast with a single pair has nothing to adjust.

Note

Every combination of levels needs at least one animal; otherwise the tool names the missing combination instead of fitting the model. With three or more factors the ANOVA table is shown without pairwise comparisons.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text:
A two-way ANOVA of RER with the factors Genotype (WT / KO) and Treatment (Control / Treated):

  1. Main effects and interaction. Genotype p = 0.725, Treatment p = 0.808, Genotype × Treatment p = 0.228: none is significant, and the partial eta-squares are small. Neither factor shifts RER, and the treatment does not act differently in the two genotypes.
  2. Post-hoc. The pairwise comparisons show small mean differences, all p > 0.05, low Hedges g and Bayes factors below 1 — no pair of groups differs.

RER is the same across the four groups, with no interaction between genotype and treatment.

items.title: Non-parametric Tests
items.text:
The non-parametric tests compare groups on the ranks of the values instead of the values themselves, so they do not assume normally distributed data — the route of steps 15–21 of Speakman et al. (2013) when a variable stays non-normal even after a transformation. The factor decides the design:

  • a between-subject factor compares independent groups — the Mann–Whitney U test for two groups, the Kruskal–Wallis H test for more, followed by Dunn's test or pairwise Mann–Whitney tests;
  • a within-subject factor compares the same animals across its levels — the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for two levels, Friedman's test for more, followed by pairwise Wilcoxon tests.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable to compare.
  • Factor — any factor but Animal and Total (Common settings): between-subject for independent groups, within-subject (such as the light cycle) for repeated measurements of the same animals.
  • Post-hoc test — for three or more independent groups: Dunn's test (on the ranks of all animals) or Pairwise Mann–Whitney U. Paired designs always use pairwise Wilcoxon tests.
  • P-value adjustment — the correction of the pairwise p-values (Holm's step-down Bonferroni by default).

The analysis uses one value per animal and level: the variable aggregated over the rows with its aggregation. Paired tests use the animals that have a value in every level; the others are left out, with a note.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• Medians and quartiles of each level: n, median, Q1, Q3.
  • The test — Test, n, Statistic (U, H, V — the sum of the positive ranks — or χ²), DF, p_unc and an effect size: the rank-biserial correlation r_rb for two levels, epsilon2 (ε²) for Kruskal–Wallis, Kendall's W for Friedman. Method tells whether the p-value is exact or the normal approximation with a continuity correction, as R's wilcox.test decides: exact below 50 animals per group when there are no ties.
  • The post-hoc tests (three or more levels): for each pair of levels A and B, Dunn's z with the mean ranks, or the pairwise test's statistic with the medians, p_unc, and the adjusted p_corr.
  • The figure — a box plot per level with the animals' values; in a paired design, lines join each animal's values.

items.title: Reading the result
items.text:
1. Test. A p_unc below 0.05 means at least one level differs from the others; the effect size says how strongly the ranks separate (ε² and Kendall's W run from 0 to 1, r_rb from −1 to 1).
  2. Post-hoc. With three or more levels, the pairs whose p_corr is below 0.05 are the ones that differ.
  3. Medians. Report the medians and quartiles, not the means: the tests compare distributions, not means.

The tests cannot correct for body size: when groups also differ in body mass, a skewed variable is better transformed and analysed with the ANCOVA (steps 3 and 15 of the paper).

In a pipeline the node publishes the test's p-value as p, which a Decision node can route on.

items.title: One-way ANOVA
items.text: One-way ANOVA tests whether the mean of a variable differs between the levels of one between-subject factor, by partitioning the variance into a between-group and a within-group part. TSE Analytics checks the assumptions first and picks the matching test: the classic ANOVA with Tukey-HSD post-hoc tests when the variances are equal, Welch's ANOVA with Games-Howell post-hoc tests when they are not.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable whose means are compared.
  • Factor — a between-subject factor with two or more levels.
  • Effect size — the effect size reported with each pairwise comparison (see Toolbox).

The analysis uses one value per animal: the variable aggregated over the animal's rows with its aggregation.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• Univariate normality test (Shapiro–Wilk) per level: W, pval, normal (True when the level's values pass). A level with fewer than four animals is not tested: its W and pval stay empty.
  • Homoscedasticity (Levene's test, centred on the median): W, pval, equal_var. Animals without a value are left out.
  • One-way classic ANOVA (equal variances): Source, SS (sums of squares), DF, MS (mean squares), F, p_unc (the p-value), np2 (partial eta-square). Then Pairwise Tukey-HSD post-hoc tests: for each pair of levels A and B their means mean_A and mean_B, diff (mean_A − mean_B), se, T, p_tukey (the corrected p-value) and the chosen effect size.
  • One-way Welch ANOVA (unequal variances): Source, ddof1, ddof2, F, p_unc, np2. Then Pairwise Games-Howell post-hoc tests with the same columns, plus df, and pval in place of p_tukey.
  • The multiple comparisons plot: the mean of each level with its Tukey confidence interval; two levels whose intervals do not overlap differ significantly.

Note

The p-value correction of the pairwise comparisons follows the chosen test (Tukey-HSD or Games-Howell) and is not adjustable here; the P-value adjustment setting belongs to the other ANOVAs.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text:
In an experiment comparing the respiratory exchange ratio (RER) of a wild-type (WT) and a knockout (KO) genotype:

  1. Assumptions. Both WT (p = 0.234) and KO (p = 0.157) pass the normality test, and Levene's test gives p = 0.283: the variances do not differ, so the classic ANOVA applies.
  2. ANOVA. F = 0.111 with p = 0.746: the difference in RER between the genotypes is not significant, and the effect size η² = 0.011 says genotype explains about 1 % of the variance.
  3. Post-hoc. The Tukey comparison of WT and KO confirms it: p = 0.746, a mean difference of 0.005 and Hedges g = 0.18.

The genotypes have practically the same RER; the experiment gives no evidence of a genotype effect on RER.

items.title: Repeated Measures ANOVA
items.text: Repeated measures ANOVA tests whether a variable changes across repeated measurements of the same animals — the days of a protocol, the light and dark phases, the intervals of a day — using one or two within-subject factors.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Dependent variable — the variable to test.
  • Within-subject factors — tick one or two within-subject factors, such as Days, LightCycle or a time-interval factor (see Time grouping).
  • Pairwise tests — untick to skip the post-hoc comparisons: their number grows with the square of the number of levels, and a factor with many intervals can take minutes.
  • Effect size and P-value adjustment — for the pairwise comparisons.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• Sphericity test (Mauchly), one per factor: Sphericity (True when the variances of the differences between all pairs of levels are equal), W, Chi-square, DOF, p-value. A factor with two levels is spherical by definition.
  • Repeated measures ANOVA, one factor: rows for the factor and its Error, with SS, DF, MS, F, p_unc, ng2 (generalized eta-square) and eps (the Greenhouse-Geisser epsilon). When the sphericity test fails, the table adds p_GG_corr (the Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-value — use it then) and the sphericity statistics sphericity, W_spher and p_spher. Two factors: a row per factor and for their interaction, with SS, ddof1, ddof2, MS, F, p_unc, p_GG_corr, ng2 and eps (1 for a factor with two levels).
  • Pairwise post-hoc tests: each pair of levels with mean_A, std_A, mean_B, std_B, Paired = True, T, dof, p_unc, with an adjustment p_corr and p_adjust, then BF10 and the effect size. With two factors, each factor's levels are compared on the animals' means over the other factor, then the interaction compares the second factor's levels within each level of the first.

Only animals with a value in every level (every combination of levels, with two factors) take part.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text:
RER recorded continuously and grouped by a time-interval factor of 8 hours:

  1. Sphericity. Sphericity = True with p = 1.0: the assumption holds and the uncorrected p-values apply.
  2. ANOVA. F = 53.2, p < 0.001: RER differs between the 8-hour intervals; the generalized eta-square of 0.726 says about 73 % of the variance is explained by the time of day.
  3. Post-hoc. Several pairs differ strongly (interval 0 versus 2, p = 0.00001; 0 versus 5, p < 0.00001), all paired, with Hedges g of 3 to 4 and Bayes factors above 1000.

RER follows a clear daily rhythm — higher carbohydrate oxidation in the active dark phase, more fat oxidation in the resting light phase.

items.title: Correlation
items.text: Correlation analysis tells whether two variables move together: the Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of their linear relationship, and a t-test tells whether it differs from zero.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• X variable and Y variable — the two variables; every row of the datatable is one pair.
  • Group by — colours the points and the marginal distributions per animal or per level of a factor (Total: one colour). The tables always use all rows.

items.title: Result
items.text:
The joint plot shows the pairs as points with the marginal distribution of each variable along its axis — a histogram for a single group, one density curve per group otherwise.

The Pearson correlation table, over all rows with both values: n (the number of pairs), r (the coefficient, from −1 to +1), CI95 (its 95 % confidence interval), p_unc (the p-value), BF10 (the Bayes factor for a correlation) and power (from five pairs on). The t-test table compares the two variables' means: T, dof (Welch's when the two variables have a different number of values), p_val, CI95 of the difference, cohen_d, power and BF10.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text: A correlation of drinking and feeding with r = 0.6 and p < 0.001 says the two go up and down together across the recording — as expected for animals that drink while they eat — and r explains 36 % (r²) of the variance of one by the other. An r close to zero with a wide confidence interval means few pairs or no linear relationship; the colours of the joint plot show whether the groups follow one trend or several before you conclude.

items.title: Regression
items.text: Linear regression fits a straight line of a response variable against a covariate, separately within each group, and tests whether the slope differs from zero.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Covariate — the predictor on the x-axis.
  • Response — the variable on the y-axis.
  • Group by — one fit per level of a factor, or one for all animals (Total).

Every point is one animal: both variables aggregated over the animal's rows with their aggregations.

items.title: Result
items.text:
The plot shows the points and the fitted line per group. The regression table gives, per group and coefficient (Intercept and the covariate): coef (the estimate), se, T, pval, r2 and adj_r2 (how much of the response the line explains), and CI2.5 / CI97.5, the bounds of the coefficient's 95 % confidence interval. A group with fewer than three animals gets a note instead of a table: two points always fit a line exactly.

A significant slope for the covariate with a reasonable r2 means the response changes with the covariate in that group; compare the slopes between groups to see whether the relationship differs — the ANCOVA tests that formally.

items.title: Actogram
items.text: The actogram is the classic picture of a rhythm: every day of the recording is one row, the activity of each bin a mark, and each row is plotted twice (the day and the following day side by side) so that patterns crossing midnight stay visible.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the activity variable to plot.
  • Bins per hour — the resolution of the marks (6 by default, ten-minute bins).

items.title: Result
items.text: One actogram per animal, in the animal's colour. A stable nocturnal rhythm shows as a dark band in the same hours every day; a band that shifts from row to row shows a free-running rhythm; scattered marks show a fragmented one. The double plot makes a band that starts in the evening and ends after midnight appear as one continuous block.

items.title: Chronobiology
items.text: The Chronobiology tool measures the circadian rhythm of a variable: how strong it is, when its peak falls, and when the activity starts and stops each day. It fits cosinor curves, computes a periodogram and detects the daily onset and offset per group.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the rhythmic variable: activity (DistD, XT+YT), feeding, drinking, energy expenditure.
  • Group by — one analysis per animal, per level of a factor, or one for all (Total).
  • Period [h] — the period of the main cosinor fit, 24 h for a circadian rhythm.
  • Second period [h] — a second harmonic, 12 h by default, that captures a bimodal day.
  • Bins per hour — the resolution the data is binned to before the analysis (1 by default).
  • Onset threshold [%] — the fraction of the daily peak that counts as the start and end of the active phase.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• The cosinor fit per group: the mesor (the rhythm-adjusted mean), the amplitude (half the peak-to-trough difference), the acrophase (the time of the peak) and the goodness of fit, with the fitted curve over the mean day.
  • The periodogram: the power at each period, with the dominant period marked (see Periodogram).
  • The activity onset and offset per day and group, and their regularity.

A high amplitude relative to the mesor and an acrophase in the dark phase describe a healthy nocturnal rhythm; a flat curve or a drifting onset indicates a disrupted one.

items.title: Periodogram
items.text: The periodogram tells which periods dominate a time series: it estimates, for every candidate period between the chosen bounds, how much of the variable's variance a rhythm of that period explains, using the Lomb–Scargle method, which tolerates gaps in the data.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable to analyse.
  • Group by — one periodogram per animal, per level of a factor, or one for all.
  • Min period [h] and Max period [h] — the range of periods to scan (1 to 48 hours by default).

items.title: Result
items.text: Power against period, per group, with the strongest peaks listed. A healthy circadian variable peaks at 24 h, often with a second peak at 12 h; a peak elsewhere, or no clear peak, points to a disrupted or free-running rhythm. Use at least three full days of data for a reliable 24-hour peak.

items.title: Facet Plot
items.text: The Facet Plot compares group means side by side: a grid of bar plots with error bars, one panel per level of a second factor.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable whose mean is plotted.
  • Group by — the factor (or Animal) that defines the bars within a panel.
  • Facet by — the factor whose levels become the panels; LightCycle by default, so each panel is a light or dark phase.

items.title: Result
items.text: One bar per group in every panel, with the mean over all rows of that group and facet and an error bar. Compare bars within a panel to compare the groups under one condition; compare panels to see how the condition changes the picture.

items.title: Fast Line Plot
items.text: The Fast Line Plot draws one variable over the whole recording, fast enough to scroll through days of one-minute data. Use it to spot artefacts, gaps and patterns before any analysis.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
The toolbar above the plot applies changes at once — there is no Update button:

  • Variable — the variable to draw.
  • Group by — Animal (one line per animal) or a factor (one line per level, the mean of its animals).
  • Scatter plot — points instead of lines.
  • Animal filter — when grouping by animal, tick the animals to show; Clear shows all again.
  • Add Report — a snapshot of the chart goes into a report.

items.title: Reading the plot
items.text: The upper chart is the detail; the lower one shows the whole recording with the window the detail covers. Drag the window, or drag inside the detail chart to zoom into a span. The choices are remembered per user.

items.title: See also
items.text: • Line Plot — group means with error bands, for a report

items.title: Line Plot
items.text: The Line Plot draws several variables over time as group means with an error band, with the dark phases shaded. It is the plot for a report; for browsing a long recording use the Fast Line Plot.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick the variables to draw; each gets its own panel.
  • Group by — Animal (one line per animal) or a factor (one line per level, the mean of its animals).
  • Error bar — the band around a group mean: None, Confidence Interval, Percentile Interval, Standard Error (the default) or Standard Deviation. No band is drawn for a group with one animal.
  • Line width — in points.

items.title: Result
items.text: One panel per variable, time on the x-axis, one line per group with its band, and the dark phases of the light cycle shaded. At one-minute intervals over several days the plot is dense; resample the datatable to an hourly interval for a clearer picture (Deriving a datatable).

items.title: Composite Performance Score
items.text: The Composite Performance Score ranks the animals across several variables at once: every chosen variable is normalised, flipped when a lower value is better, weighted, and summed into one score per animal.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick Use for every variable that enters the score; for each choose whether Higher or Lower values are better and a Weight.
  • Normalization — Z-score (each variable centred and scaled by its standard deviation) or Min-max (each variable rescaled to 0…1).
  • Color by — the factor that colours the animals in the plot.

items.title: Result
items.text: A ranked bar chart of the scores, one bar per animal coloured by the chosen factor, and the table of the scores with the contribution of every variable. The score has no unit: it says how an animal compares with the others of the datatable on the chosen variables, not how it would compare in another dataset.

items.title: Distribution
items.text: The Distribution tool shows how the values of one variable are spread within each group and where the groups overlap, as violin, box or raincloud plots side by side.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable to plot.
  • Group by — one plot per animal, per level of a factor, or one for all rows.
  • Plot type — Violin plot, Box plot or Raincloud plot.
  • Show points — draw the individual values as well.

items.title: Reading the plots
items.text:
• A box plot shows the interquartile range (the box, from the first to the third quartile), the median (the line inside), whiskers to the furthest value within 1.5 × IQR, and the values beyond as points.
  • A violin plot adds the density of the values: the wider the violin, the more values at that level. A box plot sits inside it.
  • A raincloud plot puts the density, the box and the points next to each other.

Groups whose boxes do not overlap are likely to differ; a violin with two bulges hints at two sub-populations, or at a light–dark difference that the grouping does not separate.

items.title: Histogram
items.text: A histogram shows how the values of one variable are distributed: the range of values on the x-axis, cut into bins, and how many rows fall into each bin on the y-axis.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable to plot.
  • Group by — one histogram per animal, per level of a factor, or one for all rows (Total).

items.title: Result
items.text: One histogram per group, each with its own axis range fitted to its data. Compare the shapes — a single peak, two peaks, a long tail — rather than the bar heights across panels, since the scales differ.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text: In a histogram of animal speed (cm/s on the x-axis, frequency on the y-axis), animals whose distribution peaks near 0 cm/s remained mostly inactive during the observation period, while animals with a wider range of speed values were more active. A histogram is the quickest way to see whether a group behaves as one population or as two.

items.title: Normality
items.text: Many statistical tests — the ANOVA family, the t-test, linear models — assume normally distributed data. The Normality tool draws a Q–Q plot per group so you can judge the assumption before running them.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable to test.
  • Group by — one plot per animal, per level of a factor, or one for all rows.

items.title: Reading the plot
items.text: Each point is one value, standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: its observed quantile on the y-axis against the quantile a normal distribution would give on the x-axis; the points of a panel take the colour of its animal or level. Points on the grey 45° line mean a normal distribution; the red best-fit line, its dashed 95 % confidence band and the coefficient of determination R² summarise how close the points come. The square axes always show every point. An S-shaped curve means heavier or lighter tails than normal; a bend at one end means skew.

items.title: Example interpretation
items.text: For a variable such as CenA (central ambulatory beam interruptions), points that follow the 45° line and stay inside the confidence band, with an R² above 0.9, can be treated as approximately normal, and parametric tests apply. Values that peel away at the upper end indicate a long tail — consider a transformation, a non-parametric test, or grouping by light cycle if the tail is the dark-phase activity.

items.title: Correlation Matrix
items.text: The correlation matrix shows which variables carry the same information: a heatmap of the pairwise Pearson correlations of the chosen variables, computed over all rows of the datatable.

items.title: Settings
items.text: • Variables — tick two or more variables.

items.title: Result
items.text: A square heatmap, one cell per pair, coloured from −1 (perfect negative correlation) through 0 to +1, with the coefficient printed in the cell. Strongly correlated variables are redundant for a PCA or a composite score; a pair with a surprising sign is worth a look in the Correlation tool.

items.title: Matrix Plot
items.text: The matrix plot shows how every pair of the chosen variables relates: a grid with one panel per pair, coloured by group.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick two or more variables.
  • Group by — the colour of the points: per animal, per level of a factor, or one colour for all.
  • Plot type — Scatter Plot, Histogram, Kernel Density Estimate or Regression (a scatter with a fitted line per group) in the off-diagonal panels; the diagonal shows each variable's distribution.

items.title: Result
items.text: Rows and columns are the variables; each off-diagonal panel plots the row variable against the column variable. Read the grid for pairs that line up (correlated), that split by colour (a group difference) or that spread without structure.

items.title: MDS
items.text: Multidimensional scaling places the rows in two dimensions so that the distances between them match the distances in the space of the chosen variables as closely as possible. Rows that are far apart in the plot really are dissimilar.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick three or more variables.
  • Group by — the colour of the points.
  • Components — 2 for a plot.
  • Max iterations — the optimisation budget.
  • Metric — the distance between rows (euclidean by default).

items.title: Result
items.text: A scatter plot of the embedding, with the stress — how well the plotted distances reproduce the true ones (lower is better). Unlike t-SNE, the distances in the plot are meaningful, so the separation between two groups can be read as the difference between them.

items.title: PCA
items.text: Principal component analysis finds the combinations of the chosen variables that explain most of their variance, and projects every row onto the first two of them. It shows the main axes along which the animals or groups differ without picking a variable in advance.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick three or more variables.
  • Group by — the colour of the points: per animal, per level of a factor, or one colour for all.

items.title: Result
items.text:
• The scatter plot of the rows on the first two components: PC1 on the x-axis captures the largest share of the variance, PC2 on the y-axis the largest share of what is left. Points close together are similar in the chosen variables; groups that separate along an axis differ in the variables that load on it.
  • The explained variance ratio per component tells how much of the structure the plot keeps; two components explaining 90 % or more mean the picture is faithful.
  • The loadings tell which variables make up each component.

Note

The variables are standardised before the analysis, so a variable with a large range does not dominate. Highly correlated variables (see the Correlation Matrix) share a component.

items.title: t-SNE
items.text: t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding projects the rows into two dimensions while keeping neighbours together: rows that are similar in the chosen variables end up close in the plot. It reveals local clusters that a PCA, which preserves the global variance, can miss.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick three or more variables.
  • Group by — the colour of the points.
  • Components — 2 for a plot.
  • Perplexity — roughly the number of neighbours each point considers (30 by default); use a smaller value for small datasets, and try several — the picture changes with it.
  • Max iterations — the optimisation budget.
  • Metric — the distance between rows (euclidean by default).

items.title: Result
items.text: A scatter plot of the embedding. Distances between clusters and the axes have no meaning; only the grouping does. Points of one colour that form their own cluster indicate a group with a distinct profile across the chosen variables. Run it twice with different perplexities before drawing conclusions.

items.title: UMAP
items.text: Uniform manifold approximation and projection embeds the rows in two dimensions, keeping both the local neighbourhoods and more of the global layout than t-SNE. It is fast enough for large datatables.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variables — tick three or more variables.
  • Group by — the colour of the points.
  • Neighbors — how many neighbours define the local structure (15 by default); smaller values show finer clusters, larger values more of the global shape.
  • Components — 2 for a plot.
  • Metric — the distance between rows.
  • Min distance — how tightly points may pack (0.1 by default); smaller values give denser clusters.

items.title: Result
items.text: A scatter plot of the embedding. As with t-SNE, the axes have no unit; look for groups that occupy their own region.

items.title: Learning Curve
items.text: The Learning Curve shows whether performance improves over the course of the experiment: a chosen metric is computed per animal in successive bins of time or of visits, plotted as a curve, and summarised by the slope of each animal's curve.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Metric — % Correct visits, Place-error rate, Nosepoke error rate or Licks per visit.
  • Bin by — Time interval or Visit block.
  • Bin size — hours per bin, or visits per block (24 by default).
  • Group by — the curves per animal, or the mean curve per level of a factor.

The tool needs an IntelliCage (or IntelliMaze) dataset.

items.title: Result
items.text: The learning curves with the metric against the bin, and the table of per-animal slopes with their significance. A positive slope of % Correct visits (or a negative slope of an error rate) means the animal learned the task; the group means show whether one group learned faster.

items.title: Place Preference
items.text: The Place Preference tool tests whether animals prefer particular corners: a chi-square test on the visit counts per corner, and a Kruskal–Wallis test on the visit durations.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Correct place, Neutral place, Incorrect place — which corners count as the correct ones in the protocol (the neutral and incorrect corners can be counted as correct too).
  • Exclude visits — leave out the correct or the incorrect visits.
  • Only visits with nosepokes and Only visits with licks — restrict the analysis to visits in which the animal poked or drank.

The tool needs the Visits datatable of an IntelliCage (or IntelliMaze) dataset.

items.title: Result
items.text: Per animal, the visit counts and durations per corner, the chi-square test on the counts and the Kruskal–Wallis test on the durations, with the fraction of correct visits. A significant chi-square with most visits in the correct corner shows a learned preference.

items.title: Transitions
items.text: The Transitions tool tests whether an animal moves between the corners of the IntelliCage in a non-random pattern. It counts, for every animal, how often a visit to one corner is followed by a visit to each other corner, and tests the transition matrix with a chi-square test.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Alpha — the significance level (0.05 by default).
  • Include diagonal — count repeated visits to the same corner as transitions.

The tool needs the Visits datatable of an IntelliCage (or IntelliMaze) dataset.

items.title: Result
items.text: Per animal, the transition matrix as a heatmap (from-corner by to-corner), the chi-square statistic and its p-value. A p-value below alpha means the animal's corner sequence is not random — a preference for a corner, or a fixed route, as in a place-preference protocol.

items.title: Autocorrelation
items.text: Autocorrelation measures how long one animal's time series stays correlated with its own past: the correlation of the series with itself shifted by one row, two rows, and so on. The partial autocorrelation removes the influence of the shorter lags to show the direct dependence at each lag.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable to analyse.
  • Animal — the single animal to analyse.

items.title: Result
items.text: Two plots in the animal's colour, the autocorrelation function (ACF) and the partial autocorrelation function (PACF), with the correlation from −1 to +1 on the y-axis against the lag on the x-axis and a confidence band around zero. A bar outside the band is a significant correlation at that lag. A slow decay of the ACF means a smooth, persistent signal; a peak at the lag of one day means a daily rhythm; a PACF that cuts off after a few lags means the series depends only on its recent past.

items.title: Decomposition
items.text: Seasonal decomposition splits one animal's time series into three parts: the trend (the slow movement), the seasonal component (the repeating daily cycle) and the residual (what is left — noise and irregular events).

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Variable — the variable to decompose.
  • Animal — the single animal to analyse; time-series analyses work on one series at a time.
  • Period — the length of one cycle in rows of the datatable: 1440 for a daily cycle at one-minute intervals, 24 at hourly intervals.
  • Method — Naive (moving averages) or STL (smoothing) (seasonal-trend decomposition by Loess, robust to outliers).
  • Model (naive method only) — Additive, when the cycle's amplitude stays the same over the recording (Y = T + S + R), or Multiplicative, when it grows with the level (Y = T × S × R).

items.title: Result
items.text: Four panels in the animal's colour: the observed series, the trend, the seasonal component and the residual. A clean daily cycle appears as a regular seasonal panel; a trend that rises or falls over days shows habituation or a treatment effect; large residuals mark the times when something unusual happened.

items.title: Workspace tree
items.text: The Datasets tree in the sidebar shows everything the workspace holds and is where you select what to work with, open it, and edit, clone, delete or merge it.

items.title: What the tree shows
items.text:
• Dataset — one import or merge, with a checkbox for merging. Its children:
    • datatables — Main (the table every analysis starts from) and the datatables you derive from it or add from analysis results;
    • Raw Data — the extension tables of the export (DrinkFeed, Calo, ActiMot, Group Housing; the modules of an IntelliMaze export), grouped by extension. A table with a puzzle icon has a viewer;
    • Reports — the dataset's reports, with the date they were created;
    • Pipelines — the dataset's pipelines (internal feature).

Select a row with a click; the sidebar's Info, Animals and Factors tabs follow the selected dataset, and the Toolbox menu acts on the selected datatable. Double-click a datatable, raw table, report or pipeline (or press Enter) to open it as a panel; → and ← expand and collapse a row.

items.title: Toolbar
items.text:
• Import ▾ — Import dataset… (see Importing data); with internal features on, also the import of extension data from CSV into the selected dataset.
  • Edit — the Edit Dataset dialog for a dataset, the Edit Datatable dialog for a datatable.
  • Clone — a copy of the selected dataset or datatable, under a name you choose (… (clone) by default).
  • Delete — removes the selected dataset, datatable, raw table, report or pipeline after a confirmation.
  • Merge — enabled once two or more datasets are ticked; see Merging datasets.

items.title: Context menus
items.text:
Right-click a row for the same commands and a few more:

Row Commands Dataset Edit…, Clone…, Delete; with internal features: New Pipeline…, Import Pipeline…, the four Import … data… commands Datatable Open, Edit…, Rename…, Clone…, Delete Raw table Open, Delete Report Open, Rename…, Clone…, Delete Pipeline Open, Rename…, Clone…, Export…, Delete

Warning

Deleting removes the item from the workspace with everything that belongs to it — a dataset takes its datatables, raw tables, reports and pipelines along. There is no undo; the file the dataset was imported from is not touched.

items.title: See also
items.text:
• Dataset details — the Info, Animals and Factors tabs
  • Data table — what opens when you double-click a datatable

items.title: Deriving a datatable
items.text:
Edit on a datatable does not change it: the Edit Datatable dialog creates a new datatable derived from the selected one, so the original stays available. Use it to analyse the same data at another sample interval or without some animals.

  • Name — the new datatable's name (… (derived) by default) and Description.
  • Exclude animals — tick the animals to leave out.
  • Resampling — tick it and choose a number of days, hours or minutes to aggregate the rows to that interval, each variable with its own aggregation (see Variables).

Click OK: the new datatable appears under the dataset, next to Main, and opens like any other. It keeps the dataset's animals, factors and outlier settings.

Other ways to get a datatable:

  • Clone… in the tree copies a datatable as it is.
  • Results ▸ Add as Datatable… in an analysis tool turns a result table into a datatable (see Toolbox).
  • The Add Datatable button of the DrinkFeed and Group Housing viewers stores their processed data (see Extension viewers).

items.title: See also
items.text: • Editing a dataset — the same operations applied to the dataset itself, permanently

items.title: Editing a dataset
items.text:
Edit (or Edit… in the context menu) on a dataset opens the Edit Dataset dialog, which changes the dataset itself: its name, its sample interval, its time range and its animals. Tick the sections you want and click OK; they are applied in the order shown.

  • Rename — a new name for the dataset. Names are unique within the workspace.
  • Apply resampling — a new sample interval (a number of days, hours or minutes). Every datatable of the dataset is aggregated to that interval with the aggregation of each variable (mean, sum, max, …; see Variables). The interval cannot be shorter than the recorded one.
  • Trim time — a new start and end; data before the start and after the end is dropped. Both must lie within the recording.
  • Exclude time — a time span inside the recording that is dropped, for example a maintenance break.
  • Exclude animals — tick the animals to remove from the dataset with all their data. Click a column header to sort the list.

Warning

These changes cannot be undone: the dropped rows and animals are gone from the workspace. Clone the dataset first (Clone in the tree) if you may need the original again. The file you imported from is never changed.

Tip

To keep the dataset as it is and analyse a resampled or filtered variant next to it, derive a datatable instead: see Deriving a datatable.

items.title: See also
items.text: • Merging datasets — merging needs matching sample intervals and animals; edit the datasets first

items.title: Merging datasets
items.text: Two or more datasets of the same design — the same cohort recorded in several trials, or several cohorts of one study — can be merged into one dataset with a Trial factor that tells the trials apart.

items.title: Merge
items.text:
1. Tick the checkbox of every dataset to merge in the tree, then click Merge in the toolbar.
  2. Fill in the dialog and click Merge. The merge runs in the background; the new dataset appears in the tree when it is done. The original datasets stay.
  • The table lists the datasets with their recording start and end; they are merged in the order of their start.
  • Name — the merged dataset's name.
  • Continuous — the rows keep their recorded date and time, so the trials follow each other on the time axis.
  • Overlap — the rows are aligned by the time elapsed since each trial's start, so the trials lie on top of each other. Tick Add trial number as suffix in animal names when the trials reuse the same animal ids (the animals become 1001-1, 1001-2, …); otherwise the same id in two trials is treated as the same animal.
  • Merge as a single trial — no Trial factor is created; the rows of all datasets are one trial.

The merged dataset has a Trial column and factor (unless merged as a single trial), the union of the raw tables, and the animals and factors of the sources.

Note

The datasets need the same variables and the same sample interval. Use Edit Dataset to resample or trim a dataset first, and Reset in the Variables panel if the variable settings differ.
